utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have one procedural matter to deal with before we start this morning. In the course of evidence on - and I'm just -- have lost the date for the moment - the 14th of September, pages 3439 and 40, an exhibit was admitted under seal; it was a war diary with the number 2297. The Prosecution have now advised that there is no reason why it should remain under seal. It can be made public. Intimation of that should have been given to the Defence. If there's nothing to be said by anyone for any of the accused on the matter, then it's our proposal to make that a public exhibit. Very well. That will happen. Mr. Marcussen, who's your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one matter that should be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll recall last week I objected to the transcript, using the word "diffuse" when the witness said "defuse" and Your Honour indicated there may not be any difference. Just -- and I said it was important and I still believe that and so I want to share with you the definition of those words. D-i-f-f-u-s-e, which was the word that went in the transcript, means to pour out and spread, like a fluid, or to spread or scatter widely or thinly. That is not what the witness was talking about, doing something like that. Defuse, d-e-f-u-s-e, the dictionary definition is to make less dangerous, tense or embarrassing, which is what the witness was talking about, to try to reduce the tension and make things more -- less dangerous. So this could be important not for this Chamber but for a future Chamber where there would be an argument about what the witness said in that regard. So I think that needs to be corrected and the proper word needs to be put in the transcript at the appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think as I said at the time, Mr. Ackerman, the Trial Chamber noted the point and will take account of the submission that's made about exactly what the witness said and will reflect also upon the comments that you've made at this moment. It is a matter to which you will no doubt draw attention when you make submissions in due course. Now, Mr. Marcussen, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The Prosecution's next witness is Major General John Karol Drewienkiewicz. We're proposing the witness as a combined 92 ter and live witness. And I should say that I have indicated to the Defence that we would seek leave for good measure to amend the 65 ter summary on one point. Why we need to seek leave is unclear but I think I should do it for -- to be on the safe side. We would ask that we be allowed to lead evidence about a notebook recording on an intercept -- an intercepted communication involving Sainovic, involving the event at Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you say communication about Mr. Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In which Mr. Sainovic is appearing. It's an intercept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean an intercepted communication in which he is one of the communicators?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- I'm very sorry about that. I had no idea there was an issue over amendment to the 65 ter summary. We are constantly being faced with unexpected procedural issues in this trial, and I would not have arranged for you to come into the court had I known this, so could you please leave us for the moment. There was no notice given of this, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, it was noted in the witness notification that was filed last week, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That there would be a motion to amend the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think after the heading 65 ter summary, there's a heading saying additional issues in which we say the Prosecution will seek leave to lead evidence regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I read as much as I can, but unless something like that is specifically highlighted, it's not necessarily going to come to my attention. Anyway, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this appeal by the OTP to amend their 65 ter list and their wish to lead evidence on the circumstances. There is -- there are a whole spectrum of reasons for that but I just want to say the following. This witness provided a 40-page statement six years ago. He testified for several hours about Racak four years ago. He had plenty of opportunity to say what he had to say on the topic. He came here on the 20th of November, and now we have a piece of paper which is allegedly an extract, an exert from his diary. It doesn't have a heading, a signature, or a date. It only contains the following sentences -- I'm trying to read his handwriting. [In English] Intercept appears to have got the full transcript of the unit that did the massacre. [Interpretation] That was the first sentence. The second one: [In English] -- is mentioned I think. [Interpretation] Based on these two sentences, it seems that the OTP wishes to lead evidence about an alleged conversation in which Sainovic participated, thus implicating him directly and this and that, all this coming from those two sentences alone. This is far insufficient an indication. I don't believe it to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Where, Mr. Marcussen, is this document in the papers I have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is listed in the updated witness notification as Exhibit P2534.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can I see it, please, on the screen. And this is a record of what exactly, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I intended to ask the witness about this. This is an -- it's an entry in the witness's notebook from -- it's believed to be around the 20th of January. I don't think -- well, I should let the witness speak to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was he interviewed about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I mean, we -- it came up during proofing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, on the -- he was interviewed on the 20th of November, according to Mr. Petrovic. This is when it emerged, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I'd like to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you made a statement about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have not. We have informed the Defence about this in a supplemental information sheet that we provided to the Defence after the proofing. We don't file these but we provide them to the Defence. The notebook itself was disclosed to the three original accused in 2002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, maybe the Prosecution should have read it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the reason why it didn't come up in the Milosevic case was the focus there probably was on Milosevic. So in response to my learned friends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was Sainovic not one of the joint criminal enterprise in the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, no, of course he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. A lot of evidence in this case about a man called Djordjevic who's not on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In addition, there have been other evidence emerging during this trial about the existence of such an intercept, and we propose to lead this evidence, both for whatever the witness can say about the contents of the intercept but also as evidence of its mere existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you in your submission earlier mention a name when you said that you sought to lead evidence about a notebook record and an intercepted communication? Did you mention the name of another person or was it only Sainovic you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think I only mentioned Sainovic. I'll be going in the transcript to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the communication with; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It doesn't emerge from this particular entry in the notebook -- and again, we would like to explore what the witness knows about the intercept. The witness might only know about the existence of the intercept and not much about the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we are almost left speechless by this submission of the Prosecution, which suggests, first of all, uncertainty about whether an application to amend the 65 ter summary is necessary; then fails to indicate what the evidence that's proposed to lead is about in a way that enables us to relate it to the indictment. So this is an application which has no foundation and we refuse it. Can we now proceed with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. The first counsel to examine you this morning will be for the Prosecution, and that will be Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, General. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: My name is Karol John Drewienkiewicz. And I'm a retired major-general in the British army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, in -- on the 23rd of June, 2000, did you sign a statement that was given to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: After you gave that statement, have you had a chance to re-read the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the speakers be reminded kindly to break between questions and answers for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement at -- do you have a copy of the statement? I don't think you have.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would like, if I could, give a copy to the witness and just show one paragraph to the witness. It's P2508.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I'd ask if you could please have a look at paragraph 89 of the statement. In that statement -- in that paragraph you say that you believed that the shooting at the Panda Bar could be the result of one of three things.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you still believe that to be the case today or have you formed another view of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I have thought about it since, and I continue to think that it was not directly linked with previous events because they were all happening too quickly, one on the other. And the Kosovo Liberation Army did not really have the command and control to be able to direct an operation like this very fast. And so my inclination now about my -- the balance of my view now is that it was probably this middle thought -- that it was what I would call the routine aggravation previously planned and executed that night by coincidence. I don't think to the same degree that I did at the time that it was -- it was carried out by the Serbs either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from this slight modification to your views, does the statement correctly reflect the events as you remember them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does. I mean, in particular, the time between the events, which was fairly short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So if you were asked about these events today, you would describe them as you have done in the statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, but I think I would be more inclined to feel that it was the middle of the three possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry -- sorry, no, I'm talking about the rest of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Oh, right, sorry. Yes, the rest of the statement, again, in -- at the time that I made this statement in 2000, it was about a year after the -- or a year, year and a half after the events. I had moved house a couple of times, and I did not have neatly collated all of the documents that -- that over the years have been found in various packing cases as I have unpacked after -- after another move. So it was the best I could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But you would -- you would nonetheless stand by the answers you have given in the statement today. Are there anything else you think needs to be modified in the statement than what you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, no. I think I know more now than I did then, if allowed to go through my -- the various bits of paper that I've managed to amass in my travels, but it doesn't change anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: After you gave evidence here before, did no one contact you from the Office of the Prosecution between then and this trial to go over your statement and see if things had been clarified in the interim and you had further information or you could assist further in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was brought here about two and a half weeks ago, sir, but between leaving in 2002 and about two and a half weeks ago, no, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask -- we would like to tender the witness's statement which was mentioned earlier as P2508 at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a limited objection to this document insofar as there are a -- there's a wide variety of paragraphs in the statement that deal with an event that is not in the indictment that has been specifically taken out of the indictment, Racak. We're talking about paragraphs 138 through 162 inclusive and paragraphs 180 through 181, and -- so we would object to the introduction of these matters into evidence insofar as Racak is not supposed to be one of the items that we are here to defend against. And there is also an Exhibit P85 that the same objection would reply to since it deals exclusively with that event, so I raise it at this time just for the sake of judicial economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the concern that I have about the exhibit actually flows from what the general said starting at page 9, line 5, this morning, about -- it was the best he could do at the time but he really didn't have, you know, all the information available to him. I don't know whether that goes to whether or not the statement should be entered or not or whether it simply goes to the weight that it may have, but I think it's quite significant. If -- instead of the statement being used the Prosecution was asking questions and he was saying, I'm not sure but it's the best I know right now, that would be pretty weightless evidence, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As to Mr. Ivetic's objection, Your Honour, we submit that the statement should be left in its entirety. The focus of the evidence of this witness is really chain of command and linkage evidence. There are facts about Racak in the statement, but they are intertwined with issues relating to who knew about the events in Racak, who gave instructions to these events, what kind of investigations were carried out, under what conditions were these investigations carried out. And we submit that those issues are important for, as I said, linkage -- whether the accused are linked to the event in Racak and what inferences might be drawn from that. Now, with respect to Mr. Ackerman's objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, the -- it may be that there is a limited number of these paragraphs that that argument does not apply to. I cannot say offhand just now. I have read them with that in mind, and my impression was that there might be a solid objection to some of them and that others do fall into the category you indicate. We're unlikely to reach this in the first session, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think that is unlikely, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at the break we'll look at that and we'll decide which of these paragraphs, if any, have to be excluded in their entirety. On Mr. Ackerman's point, what do you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There -- on that point I wish to say that the witness has confirmed that the statement as it is is a correct reflection of his recollection of the events as of today. What the witness said was that he might be able to provide further information. The witness didn't indicate any doubt as to what was the contents of the statements, so therefore I submit Mr. Ackerman's objection should be dismissed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, the actual provision of the rule which has to be satisfied before a statement is admitted in these circumstances is the following: The witness attests that the written statement or transcript - in your case it's a statement - accurately reflects that witness declaration and what the witness would say if examined. Now, are you satisfied your statement does that, or are you hesitant about saying it does that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm satisfied it does that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, we do consider that the statement in general ought to be admitted. We are satisfied that Rule 92 ter is complied with, and we're also satisfied - having reflected on it - that it is in the interests of justice to presented part of this witness's evidence in written form, knowing two things in particular: One, that the point that is made by you goes to weight; and secondly, that you will have an opportunity to cross-examine on that very point and others in due course. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, to put your evidence in context, could I ask you first to explain why the KVM was created.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I'll try to be quick. In the spring and summer of 1998, the international community became extremely concerned at the level of violence that was going on inside Kosovo and was concerned at the actions of the -- of the Serb forces, the police and the army. As a result of that, there were a number of high-level delegations that went to Serbia and expressed that concern from the different pieces of the international community, but particularly from NATO. NATO was sufficiently concerned that it issued an ACTORD [Realtime transcript read in error " act or order"], which means that it placed its forces on a higher level of alert, a much higher level of alert. And in -- as a result of the various negotiations, an agreement was reached whereby the OSCE would provide an unarmed mission inside Kosovo, which would be called the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission. That mission would be up to 2000 verifiers strong, would was formed as quickly as possible, and would have the mandate of a year. A further force that was brought into being was a NATO air verification mission, which was to be based outside Kosovo but which was to carry out air surveillance of Kosovo in support of the verifiers on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 13, line 15, the general said that NATO had issued -- and the word he used was ACTORD; it's spelled A-C-T-O-R-D. It's a term of art and has particular significance, and so it should be correct in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Issued an ACTORD. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. A-C-T-O-R-D is the NATO term for what they did at that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's short for activation order, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you accept the comment that's made by counsel. Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, the -- how was the KVM to carry out verification on the ground in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was to get there as quickly as possible, to establish itself, and to establish liaison with all of the parties, and then to report on what it saw and to attempt to help the situation to improve with a view, it must be remembered, of assisting with elections before the year was out. And so it saw itself as taking the situation that it found on arrival and helping it to improve rather than just to observe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the statement and in various documents, in the statement, for example, at paragraph 36, there's talk about the creation of base-lines for verification. Could you explain to the Court, please, what that means.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. In the negotiations that preceded the creation of the Kosovo Verification Mission, there were a number of agreements that were come to which talked about the level of forces within Kosovo, the level of police -- Serb police and Serb military forces within Kosovo, and the agreement that had been reached was that the -- those forces should be reduced to the level that they were at before the actions of the previous spring and summer had begun. Now, in order to know whether or not that was the case, it was important to know what precisely that level was. And so one of the early things that we sought to do - that I sought to do - was to obtain an accurate base-line of what was the strength of the Serb army in Kosovo, what was the strength of the Serb police in Kosovo in some detail so that we would confirm that this was indeed being adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll get back to a little more the details of a base-line later on. General, what I'd propose to do now is to essentially follow through your statement and try to cover some issues that I think arise from your statement. The first thing is in paragraph 15 of the statement there's talk about the issuance of visas to members of the KVM and requests for multi-entry visas. Were multi-entry visas actually given to KVM staff?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: About when?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It varied. Because what happened was when a member of the KVM arrived, they came in on a single-entry visa, and once they were inside Kosovo on that single-entry visa, we then had to apply to Belgrade for a multi-entry visa and that took several weeks. And while that was going on, that individual was in effect gated inside Kosovo, was not able to go down to Macedonia, was not able to go back to Vienna for meetings, and so it limited their effectiveness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you think that affected the effectiveness of KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 20 you -- you describe the meetings you had with TEC and various other authorities during your initial mission to Kosovo to try to set up the KVM. Could you tell the Court what were the kind of things you were trying to achieve during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: In the first instance, we wanted locations that we would operate out of. We also needed contracts for fuel and the like, and we needed assistance with setting up the communications. That's the sort of thing we were after. We arrived and the 15 or so of us were living in the hotel in Pristina, which was not big enough or the right place from which to operate. We needed -- with 2.000 people coming in, you needed office space for 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was assistance forthcoming?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was not very forthcoming. We were pretty much left to go out and almost knock on doors to try to find suitable locations. We did not detect any -- any willingness to make property available quickly by, if necessary, moving somebody else out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say that Andjelkovic didn't seem to have any authority. At this period were there anybody who seemed to be having authority or were it just the general situation that there was nobody to speak to really?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: At this early stage, the first person whom we met who appeared to have some ability to influence events was General Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who was he -- do you know if he was reporting to anyone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, he reported back to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You describe in some details then how meetings unfolded and you describe where the meetings took place. You had drawn a diagram of some of the important buildings in Pristina. And then towards the end of your stay there, I understand that from paragraph 26 and paragraph 27 of your statement that you went to Pec. Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sorry, let me find --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It would be on page 5 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I've managed to get it all over the place. Right. I'm back on course. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- this was very early on, and I was not formally appointed to the Kosovo Verification Mission at this stage. I was lent to Vienna, to the OSCE, to assist with planning. And the OSCE Permanent Council sent a reconnaissance party of administrators from the Permanent Council, from the OSCE secretariat, down to Pristina in order to sort out the arrival and the accommodation for the Kosovo Verification Mission. I was attached to this group with some individuals from other delegations, but I was not in charge of it. And on that basis, I spent the first days that I was down there essentially attempting to assist the administrators. As we got to the end of our time down there, which was quite short, I realised I'd only seen things inside Pristina and therefore decided I had better get outside Pristina and see what it looked like outside Pristina and borrowed a vehicle and went off on my day's trip around Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what did it look like out there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was extremely subdued. I was surprised by the lack of normal commercial activity. There were police at roadblocks throughout the area. I moved through without let or hindrance, but my impression was that everyone was lying low, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say that there were signs of looting. Could you describe those signs. What -- if you remember --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I would say there was signs of ransacking, that doors had been kicked in, windows were broken, walls had been knocked down, and so it was as though a -- a riot had gone through the place really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was that a generalised picture throughout the areas you went through or was it in certain locations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was worse in some locations. Really the further east -- sorry, the further west you went, the worse it got, and in particular around Decani it was particularly marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You also many -- you also mention that many houses had signs of burning. Do you think those signs of burning were a result of combat operations or something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I didn't think it was as a result of combat operations; I thought it was as a result of deliberate firing of the houses. I had served in Bosnia previously, and so I had a fairly good idea of the difference between recent combat operations and deliberate burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe that a little bit more. What was it about the houses that made you think that it was deliberate burning rather than combat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because it looked as though the fire had been started inside the house and had been allowed to burn, and then burned up to the roof and then the roof fell in once the rafters -- the wooden rafters caught fire, and that looks a particular way. If it had been fought over, then there would have been more evidence of shell impact rather than just the effect of burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll jump to another part of your statement. It's on page 8, where you describe the absorption process, the attempts of the KVM to absorb the KDOMs. First, maybe you could remind us what -- the KDOM, what is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Before -- over the summer, the different embassies or some of the embassies in -- that were based in Belgrade, which began to report on the situation by sending their defence and military attaches down from Belgrade reinforced their defence attaches with a number of individuals who they then equipped in four-wheel drive vehicles, and these became known as diplomatic observer missions, so they were an extension of the office of the defence attache of the relevant embassy, and they were of varying strengths and varying capabilities. But essentially they reported to the ambassador of the country in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they have any specific verification mandates that they were working under?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I never saw their specifically mandate, but I understand that they acted as extensions of their embassies in Belgrade, and therefore had legitimacy as extensions of the -- of those diplomatic entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you say that it -- at paragraph 46 you explained that it irritated or seemed to irritate the Serb authorities that the US-DOM and the EU-DOM were not absorbed by the KVM.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then you say at paragraph 48 that the absorption process was deliberately delayed. Now, that looks like sort of a contradiction, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was because you're dealing with a lot of different -- a lot of different pieces here. If I can deal with the two separately, it was the understanding that once the Kosovo Verification Mission was -- was up and running, that the KDOMs would be absorbed into it, and that was indeed the case with some of the KDOMs. And that -- there was no purpose in the KDOMs as far as we could see once we were established. The KDOMs were 10s, 20s, 30s strong; we were building up to be 2.000 strong. So why were they needed? Therefore, we wanted to get our premises contracted and established, repaired where necessary, as quickly as possible; and in doing this, we were dealing with the Serb local authorities. And therefore, it was entirely in their interest that we became effective as quickly as possible. But that did not seem to affect the degree to which they were really quite slow and unhelpful in the contracting. And so my point I was trying to make there was that although it was in everybody's interest that we got up and running as quickly as possible, we did not discern any leaning forward by the Serb authorities to help us become more effective more quickly. And it was particularly perplexing because the quicker we became effective, the quicker the role of the KDOMs would become superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was the whole of the US-KDOM and EU-KDOM absorbed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What -- did that -- what effects did that have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It confused us and it confused the authorities, and I think it confused the Kosovo Liberation Army. So I think I can say it confused everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you raise this with the US and the European Union?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. The US authorities that I dealt with, I can remember on one occasion they came in and said, Right, we need to absorb -- we need you to absorb us in the next week, and you need to provide premises for us and how quickly can you do it? And in another breath, within two or three days they were back saying, Actually, we think we'd like to be absorbed last and do everybody else first. And eventually, we did absorb a number, about half of the US-KDOM personnel, but they remained a separate entity throughout. Now, at -- when they began saying, You need to absorb us straight away, the reason why they came back and said, Actually, we think that we've changed our mind on that, was that they felt they needed to provide support to Ambassador Hill who was doing a separate set of negotiations with the Kosovo Liberation Army and the Kosovars to try to produce a deal that was acceptable to them, and it was felt that giving him US personnel to be his direct support was appropriate, and I understand that. But that finished well before Christmas of 1998, and they continued throughout -- well into March of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So it seems that you and the Serb authorities sometime after Christmas agreed on the confusion that was created by these remaining KDOMs. Did you tell anyone from the Serb authorities about your views on this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't think I ever -- I don't think I ever specifically sat down with them. You must remember that I was not the head of mission. I was -- I was, at best, number three in that mission, and there were other people who had those responsibilities. I was -- I was more concerned with what was happening on the ground and less concerned with the diplomacy of it, not being a professional diplomat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who would you say was number two in the mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The French diplomat, Ambassador Gabriel Keller was absolutely the number two, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One other question just arising from these paragraphs. In paragraph 47 your last sentence says: "It was public that the KLA was threatening to kill anyone who signed any agreements." What do you mean by "any agreements"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was -- there was a view that Ambassador Hill -- Ambassador Hill was working with all sectors of Albanian society, including Rugova, who of course was publicly determined to do everything in a non-violent way. And that was not the view of the Kosovo Liberation Army, quite clearly. And there was -- I mean, this was -- I don't remember reading it anywhere. This was a view formed among us that there was deep division inside the Kosovar Albanian camp. Nobody was really speaking for them, but the Kosovar -- the Kosovo Liberation Army were reported and goodness knows where we -- I got it from, that anyone who signed agreements with Ambassador Christopher Hill would -- would be dealt with violently by the Kosovar Albanian KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to jump ahead to paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 9, yes. At paragraph 57 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It can't be 9 if you're going ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Page 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you say that you are sure that the Serb authorities generated daily situation reports, and then you say: "This is the military way." Can you explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever I have been anywhere, you produce a daily report, which says what's happening and what you think's going to happen next. At the very least, you say what has happened, and that was certainly the case with the -- the NATO missions I have been on. It was certainly the case with the Kosovo Verification Mission that we did a daily report up to Vienna, to the Permanent Council. And on the occasions when we met with the Serb authorities, there were moments when it was quite clear that they were reading from lists of events as well, and we weren't, in the least, surprised. And I would be surprised if they hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was it also your impression that the Serb authorities that you dealt with or reported further up their chains?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I mean, I can't think of anyone who wouldn't have reported up their chains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move to the next paragraph, paragraph 58, and go a little bit into the way the KVM -- the internal workings of the KVM. You describe in this paragraph the fusion centre. What was the fusion centre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was the group of people that were not concerned with what was going on on a minute-by-minute and a day-by-day basis, which I would call the operation side. These were the people who were taking all of the information coming in and trying to put it together to form an overall picture of what was really happening and try to work out what might happen next and how we might help, where the areas were, where we could apply more effort in order to be more effective. And so they were combining, really, the sort of forward thinking, the analysis and forward thinking part of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How was the fusion centre staffed? What was all the profile of the people working in the fusion centre?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were largely people who had done analysis before, and when you talk of analysis in the military side you're talking about intelligence. And so there were intelligence -- ex-intelligence officers in this centre. But I would say that what they were dealing with was open-source information. What was of concern to us was to take all of the open-source information and to make sure it was all put together in context and in -- in so doing work out where the opportunities lay for us and where the dangers lay for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what were the sources of information that the fusion centre had to work with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It had the reports of the verifiers out on the ground. It had the media reports, it had reports from anybody it -- people stopped and talked to, which again generally came to them through -- through the verifiers and we would occasionally get stuff from NATO down in Macedonia because there was this agreement that we should ask them in -- with the -- with their ability to conduct air reconnaissance, we should ask them questions that they would be able to answer for us so that we could do our job better. Now, if I can give you an example. We were particularly keen to have aerial reconnaissance run of a particular area to see the degree of devastation that had happened in those areas. And if you looked at a particular area from the road, you could see lots of knocked-down roofs. But unless you went right into the town or village and started counting on a house-by-house basis, it was very difficult to tell the difference between a house -- a community that had got 20 or 30 per cent of its roofs burned and a community that got 80 per cent of its roofs burned. If you run aerial reconnaissance and take one photograph, you can do that in a heart beat. And so that was the sort of thing we wanted to know. We wanted to know where the areas were that had suffered most in the summer's activities. And once we knew that, we would be able to work out where the places were that needed assistance most. Because when you spoke to the locals, all of them said that their area was of course the area that needed assistance most. So it -- we needed a better way of doing it than just necessarily asking the locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there any kind of sort of topical reports created outside the fusion centre on infrastructure matters or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Once we were set up, we were -- we set up these five regional centres and each of the regional -- which corresponded to the counties. And each of these regional centres had a responsibility to say what were the needs of the people there. And so, to do that, they carried out a number of surveys. I particularly -- I remember one being done, for instance, on the railways, and that was specifically with a view to having a proper report that could be passed up to the OSCE in Vienna, possibly across to the EU, and which might then have attracted some EU funding to get the railways going again, because that was the sort of thing we were thinking of, certainly, in the early days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you also receive information on issues relating to the security of the mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. There was an extra understanding that if NATO became aware of issues which would directly affect the security of -- of the verifiers on the ground, that they would pass that to us. And in order to receive that, we had to make specific arrangements to protect that information, but it was specifically information which would essentially keep us alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To the extent you are able to, can you give an example of such information.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm -- I'm hesitating because I am -- I have obligations under my national Official Secrets Act, and therefore I'm not going to -- I'm going to try to be careful in what I say and not end up going to jail back in England. In February -- sorry, in January we had the situation of the eight VJ soldiers who were -- who were taken captive by the KLA in the area north of Mitrovica, around the Trepca mines. We were attempting to extract -- to negotiate the safe release of those eight VJ soldiers, and in order to do that I ordered some of the verifiers up into the KLA camp to make sure that the VJ soldiers, (a), were there; (b), that they were in one piece; and (c), that they and the KLA knew that there were active discussions going on in order to try to return them safely. This went on over several days and nights, and in the course of that, we received information that Serbian special forces were being moved to a position from which they could carry out a coup de main operation on the top of the hill where the Kosovo Liberation Army were. This was of direct concern to me and of direct concern to the safety of the verifiers, because if in the middle of this particular location you suddenly had a group of special forces arrive by a helicopter or by a parachute in an attempt to get their the captives out themselves, then there was highly likely to be a fire-fight and it was quite likely that verifiers as well as everybody else would be among the injured. And I was not prepared to put my people into that situation, and therefore, that -- when I received that information, I acted on it. Now, that was information which I have no idea where the heck it came from, but it was sufficiently credible for me to act on and, I was certainly alarmed for the safety of my verifiers. And in the course of the hours preceding that, I ordered those verifiers off the top of the hill because I was worried that something was going to happen that was going to put their lives in even more danger. And then there were discussions, and then I told them to go back up, and we carried on with the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So while we're on that topic, apart from pulling your verifiers back, did you pass on the information about the special forces to anybody on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This was -- this was passed to, as I recall it, both General Loncar and to Mr. Sainovic. Ambassador Gabriel Keller was dealing on a minute-by-minute basis with Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what was the result of the -- your expression of concern about these special forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The result was that there was no special -- Serb special force intervention into the process, which meant that the process of negotiation that was going on was able to continue and was eventually brought to a successful conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you know, who decided to not engage the special forces or who told you that they would not be engaged so you could pull your verifiers back?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't think of question that would be more speculative than this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a minute, please, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, until we decide whether you should be allowed to even consider answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does sound as though it's a speculative question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me break it down in some smaller bits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I understand from your answer that special forces were not sent in.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you told that special forces would not be deployed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think -- just hold on a second. The objection was I think to the start of the question "if you know who decided." Now, isn't the first thing to establish whether he knows, and once you've got an answer to that, then you can ask the question you really want to ask. That was the objection, as I understand it. Of course if you want to address it in an entirely different way, that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, if we can do it the short way, then let's do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know who -- do you know whether a decision was taken not to deploy special forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No special forces appeared on the top of that hill, and therefore we may have been completely dreaming that these things existed. However, I think what I can say is we received information which -- from a credible source that the use of special forces was being contemplated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I just stop you there because you earlier said you had no idea what the source was but the information sounded credible enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now you're saying something rather different. Unless we're talking about two different sets of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can think of two messages I received which both related to special forces during this period; both were credible, sir. As a result of that, I reported this to Ambassador Keller, and he spoke immediately to Mr. Sainovic. And I understand that he received an assurance from Mr. Sainovic that whatever was being contemplated would be put on hold and that he was content that we continue to try to resolve the situation by negotiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that answers my question. Now, I'd like to go back to what might seen a little bit of the nitty-gritty of the paperwork in KVM, and I'd like to talk to -- ask you about the ways reports were flowing from your different regional -- regional offices and up towards your headquarters and were used by the fusion centre. And for that purpose I'd like to show Exhibit P673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does this also have a DZ number in the package of material you gave us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It does not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, can you see this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I used to be able to do font 4, but I can't now. Yeah, that's better. Thank you. Yeah, I -- yeah, this is Rugova. I know about Rugova. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you about is not so much the substance of the document, but could you explain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were -- beneath the headquarters in Pristina, there were five regional centres, each run by someone who essentially reported to me. And each day, at the end of each day, they would send a daily statement of what had happened, which got to us by, I don't know, 9.00 at night, say. We then took those reports, added what we knew as well, and turned it into a -- a report that went up to Vienna, which tried to concentrate on the big issues and tried to provide some thematic view of what was going on. So this would be one of the five reports that would come in in the evening in the normal course of events. If something extraordinary happened, then obviously we would be told -- we would be alerted to it by phone or radio, and as quickly as they knew the facts they would send us a written report with the full -- with as many facts on it as they could give us. Because if it got really -- if it was a really serious incident, then we had to get the message to Vienna quickly because Vienna were also very sensitive about being blind-sided by stuff where they were rung up by the media before they were told by us. So it was important to get an early heads-up to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So this document and documents like it, they would be daily contemporaneous reports --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- from verifiers on the ground. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. But again the regional centre was taking -- I mean, Prizren had at least 250 people subordinate -- working for it. And so this is the amalgamation of all the reports of all the 250 at the end of the day. If it was a spot report in the middle of the day, it might just be sending on to us something that had came from one or two people but which was sufficiently important to need to tell us quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, from your experience on the ground in Kosovo, were these regional reports reliable reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, particularly this one because -- I mean, obviously there were -- not every one was of the same quality and the commander of the regional centre Prizren was, I would say, the best, the most organised, the most experienced of my regional centre commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you another document, that is P666.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I can get it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is something from a coordination centre. Could you explain where that fits into the reporting picture, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Beneath the -- beneath the regional centres, there were a number of coordination centres which we wanted to put one in each municipality. And eventually there were about 42 of them, I think, on the ground, but we had to build them up as people became available and as we were able to contract real estate for them, and the Orahovac coordination centre was one of the earlier ones to be set up, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did the coordination centres, did they report to the regional centres --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- or did they report to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes -- sorry. It was quite hierarchical that the coordinating centres were the people who were assigned to the regional centre. The regional centre put out coordination centres where they felt they needed them, where the centres of population were, where bad things were happening, and that was really the -- that was the choice, that was the decision of the head of the regional centre. So coordination centres reported to regional centres who reported to ourselves in Pristina, and we reported up to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the fusion centre receive the reports from the coordination centres or did they remain at a lower level?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They tended to receive the reports of the coordination centres as well because one of the things that they did was to really go through them with a fine-tooth comb to see if there was anything that had been missed or which wasn't immediately apparent, and to see if there were trends that went back. And so this was part of the information that the fusion centre was able to work on, not on a daily basis, but on a thematic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to show you a different kind of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can look at P667, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is a memorandum. I don't know if you are able to see that yet on your screen.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah. Can we go up a few fonts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe we can just zoom in on sort of the date and where it says "memorandum" and the first two paragraphs or something. It's just to allow the general to look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is a document outside what you can see, but it's signed by KVM-MUP liaison officer or the other name come up.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this kind of document, where does that fit into the -- to the whole paper processing in KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: One of the -- one of the most important functions was to liaise with the main actors, and MUP and the VJ and the KLA were, obviously, the three actors that we were particularly concerned because they had the ability to make life very difficult. And so within each -- at each level where there were -- at least level of command of the different organisations that we had to deal with, we attempted to put someone in as a permanent liaison officer so that they dealt with the same people each time. So within the regional centres, there were MUP liaison, VJ liaison, and KLA liaison. We, too, at our level had MUP liaison, VJ liaison, and KLA liaison. And I put somebody specifically in charge of that group of liaison officers, because we understood that they were particularly important. And so, such a report would be a report rendered at any moment that it was thought that there was something useful to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would this also be fed to the fusion centre for processing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, the mission also generated a number of daily updates --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like if we could call up P657, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, these reports, who generated a daily report like this one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The report -- the daily report would be produced by a team of specific report writers of about two or three, who -- who were attached to the office of the head of mission, and the head of mission, obviously, signed off, approved the report, before it went up to Vienna every day, although sometimes if it wasn't a controversial day, he would let it go; but if it was a controversial day he would certainly want to check it to make sure that he was comfortable with the message that was being sent to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, there were also something called mission reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we could call up Exhibit P664, please. Could you scroll up so we can see the heading? Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What were the mission reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The mission report would have been, I'm pretty sure, produced by the same people that the one you saw earlier -- a moment ago was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And who were -- who did the mission report go to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It went more widely. It went down to the regional centres so they saw what was going on so they could get the bigger picture. It went around the whole of the KVM, and it went up to Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so the daily reports and mission reports, were they based on reportings coming up through the -- your internal chain of command, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now if we can see another document, P662.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about that. It looks very similar -- well, I'll wait until it comes up. This is called an interim report, and it covers the day of the 10th of January, 1999. What caused an interim report to be generated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We started off with interim reports when we -- in the period until we were completely covering the whole of the province. We started off in the west in Prizren and Pec and worked eastwards as more people were made available to us by the participating states of the OSCE. The 2000 didn't arrive all on the same day, obviously. They were arriving at a rate of about a hundred a week. And as -- we had neither the administrative support nor the real estate to be able to put everyone down at the same moment and so we set up regional centres one at a time. And until we'd got Kosovo completely covered, I'm pretty sure we were sending out what we called interim reports which it had been explained to Vienna that there was some areas where what they were getting was the result of quite a lot of people on the ground that we could check this, and there were other areas, particularly in the east, where we'd got hardly anybody and we were having to rely on the reports that were less reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when reports were less reliable, was that reflected in the reportings up the chain? Could you try to describe the quality of information --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: If it was specifically -- if it was specifically drawn from media reports, then it would often say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not clear to me where this fits in with the other documents we've been looking at and at what level this was compiled. Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, who compiled the interim reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The interim reports became the daily reports later, once we had full coverage. We called them interim reports from the day we said we really have got to produce a daily report, which was about the sort of 25th of November or 20th of November. And they kept being called interim reports until the day that we said we think we're now fully covering the place, let's stop calling them interim reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, the last of these kind of documents I'd like to ask you about is a fusion working paper, and that has Exhibit Number P680.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could see that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, a fusion working paper, who generated these? That might be obvious, but ...

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, well, they came out of the fusion cell and were produced by the individual -- by the team in the fusion cell, which obviously was under a chief and the chief worked with me, and we would generally discuss the sort of products he was working on and the rate of production; in other words, did we want one that was immediate because there was an immediate need, or could I give him a bit longer so he could spend longer and get more indication of trends. So I was consulted over the timing and the content, the subject matter to be concentrated on. He'd then go away with his team and produce something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so, depending on the nature, these would be sort of longer-term analysis or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- analysis of specific events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And again, the material underlying these reports, would that -- that would be the kind of material that the fusion cell received. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. They would -- they would use all of the material that was passed into them that had come up from the -- from the CCs, from the RCs, from individual liaison officers. I mean, all the material, throw on to it media reports, throw on to it any TV footage that came out of the media, and everything we had they would get and then they would make the best they could of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like at this stage to tender the different reports that I have mentioned and discussed with the general. I'd also like to tender some reports that I haven't discussed but that are of the same nature. They are P659, P675, P677; they are all daily updates. And then there is a mission report in addition to the one that I mentioned, which is P665. And I'll ask that they be tendered into evidence. Now, I do not intend to go through them with the witness, at least not all of them, but I can address the relevancy of the documents if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Actually, would you like me to do that now with the witness here or should we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If you don't intend to ask him any questions about them, then there can be no prejudice to dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Some of them I will ask questions about but I think I can explain the relevancy of the document without creating any problems in terms of the integrity of the evidence. Now, if I take them in the order the documents have come up. P673, which is a daily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't expect you to be going back over the ones you've already dealt with. I'm expecting you to tell me the relevance of the ones you've just listed now which I thought you weren't going to ask him questions about and which we could fit into the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well -- okay, I was actually intending as we move through only to take up a few of these and later we will make submissions on parts of these. What I sought to establish is the reliability of the reports, and it's therefore my submission that they can be admitted on the basis of what the witness has said about the generation and concept of reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you're doing in relation to the authenticity of these, but the other equally important leg of the test for admitting any of these documents is their probative value and in particular the relevance to the issues in the indictment. Now, if you're saying that the best way of doing that is to make a written submission and to allow us to look at it and you want to use your time otherwise here, then that's fine. But at some stage we'll have to be told what's the relevance of these various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I suggest that we then do it the following way. The ones that I'm not going to touch on today specifically with the witness, we will make a written submission on those, rather than spending the Court's time talking away about the validity of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that effectively means that from your reference to P673, we should regard each of the proposed exhibits as potential exhibits for the moment until we have some indication of their relevance. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, one last document that I'd like to ask you about is the document you referred to in your statement, the blue book. What is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was -- this evolved, and as we became -- as we became more organised, I felt that we needed -- before we -- the -- the people at the top of the mission met every morning, that we all needed to have a common description of what we thought the different events were of the previous day or days in a way that was not just script but which was easier to understand. They could see where things where and where they were related to one another. Because not all of the -- not all of the people at the top of the mission spent their lives pouring over the map of Kosovo. And so I asked -- or I tasked the fusion centre to produce a pictorial version of what had happened in the last day or days in each of the regional centre areas and linking all of the events to ones that had previously taken place where that was relevant. But it was specifically a pictorial view of it. It was a PowerPoint slides with points on the map describing what had happened and where. And it was produced by the fusion centre because, frankly, they were better at PowerPoint than the operation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: These reports continued -- the blue book covered the period after the KVM left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So at that point in time, there would not have been any of your verifiers on the ground to report to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How was the report then -- or, sorry, the entries to the blue book, how were they prepared, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: On the basis of the best information we were able to get. And when we left Kosovo, we continued to talk to people by mobile phone that we'd been talking to previously by mobile phone. And we also were able to talk to people as they came out of Kosovo, and there were a number of other sources like UNHCR who were dealing with the refugees as they arrived. And so the blue book continued to attempt to -- to give as much accuracy as we could to events inside Kosovo because certainly in the first three or four weeks we were keen not just to report the sensational stuff that one person gave to a member of the media as he staggered out over the border. We were trying to give information which was confirmed by more than one source. And so in doing that, we were trying to give an indication of the reliability of some of these reports because we were very concerned that there was some very exaggerated stories coming out, and the world was working itself up into a frenzy at this stage, and it needed somebody to say, Well, this incident here appears to have been corroborated by six different sources, all of which seem to support the common theme, and so we think that the report of this incident is accurate, whereas other ones might not be so accurate. This was an attempt to -- to really talk down some of the -- some of the wilder stories that were going on, but where there was genuine substance to them to give them more weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The written statement gives the impression that this book was already in existence prior to the mission leaving. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. We evolved how we worked as we -- as events unfolded and as the needs changed. And from mid- to late January I would say, off the top of my head, we got into a good rhythm of what the documents were that were useful to the mission and to Vienna and to those we dealt with. And the blue book came out of that. And so the blue book was available, for instance, while the Rambouillet negotiations were going on in February and was useful in being able to give detail where up at Rambouillet it was not uncommon for the meeting -- the start of the meetings, the negotiations, to be delayed while one person or another would say, I can't possibly sit down and negotiate until we find out what happened last night in Pec when something awful happened. And so there would be a frantic phone call from Rambouillet saying, What the heck happened last night in Pec? And we would be able either to say, Well, this is what we know happened in Pec last night. Or, We don't think anything happened in Pec but we'll ask again. And this was part of the ability to respond quickly to that sort of question. And so, yes, we were using it before we drove out. Its purpose changed somewhat once we had driven out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a suitable time to break if you can find the point, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just to clarify the last answer and then we can break. Is it a correct understanding that the term the "blue book" sort of came about later when the daily PowerPoints and comments were compiled into one document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it became -- it was because it was put into a blue folder. It's as simple as that, and I think the first time we produced it I took it to the different members of the -- of the sort of executive group that met at 8.00 in the morning and said, Look, this is what we've produced. I think it's going to be useful. What do you think? And the head of mission said, Yes, this blue book's jolly good. Thereafter it became known as the blue book. There were moments when it probably appeared in a yellow cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to a few points about the blue book later, but let's break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You probably are aware we have to break from time to time for various reasons. This is one of these occasions. We'll be breaking for about half an hour. Could you please go with the usher meanwhile; he'll show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the objection that was taken by Mr. Ivetic to parts of the statement, we consider that from paragraph 147 to paragraph 154 should not be admitted because they plainly are matters of detail in relation to the events within the locus. The other paragraphs objected to, including the two later in the statement, will be admitted. We will note carefully those which, due to some extent, also deal with the detail and exclude obviously that detail from consideration. If in the course of either the examination or the cross-examination it becomes clear that those we have so far refused to admit could have some bearing on the issues which are relevant in the trial, then we will review that part of the decision. But that's the decision so far as we can make it on the basis of the information presently available to us. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And should -- we will replace the version of the statement in e-court with a statement that reflects your ruling as it is at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, we were -- before the break, we were talking about the blue book that at times came in a yellow binder. Now, you mentioned that you were in contact with people still in Kosovo over mobile phone. Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: All variety of people, but primarily people who had worked for us. Local people who had been contracted to be part of the Kosovo Verification Mission as interpreters or press officers or security guards, and who -- when the mission evacuated, it was essentially the internationals that left, not the locals. And so, in an attempt to find out, to stay in touch, we wanted to continue to talk to all of the people that had been working for us, and this was not just Kosovar Albanians, this was Kosovar Serbs as well. And at the time, of course, we were all convinced that the NATO bombing would be very short, that a negotiated settlement would be rapidly reached, and that we would very quickly be going back up into Kosovo but this time with a greater international presence, with other people with us, with NATO with us we expected. But we needed to stay in touch with people to see what the situation was on the ground from the first point of view that we would find when we went back, in order to prepare ourselves. I mean, you know, if there was no electricity in the towns that we went back to, then we were going to have to find generators from somewhere to take up.
