That's the sort of practical consideration that we needed -- you know, that's the first thing we were thinking of. And then as bad things happened in Kosovo, we became more aware and we then started to talk to people to try to find out exactly what was going on, so as to report it in as objective a way as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you also speak to former liaisons in -- on the Serb side or the KLA side?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the assessment of the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will ask the usher to assist me with the ELMO, please. Now, the blue book is Exhibit P407, and I've taken a page out of that because it's a rather big document. It might be easier to just look at a page this way. I think it's on the video line no longer. Can we zoom out just a little bit so we can see the whole page? Okay. I think that's -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, General, once the KVM had left Kosovo and there are reports in the blue book regarding the situation in Kosovo, to the blue book they attached these sort of tables. Could you explain what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was put in because we were dealing with a huge variety of sources, and what we were trying to do was to distinguish things that we had -- that we felt were correct because they came from someone we knew well, or they came from multiple sources or things which one person who we had never seen before in our lives told us, maybe over a mobile phone, which could have been disinformation and certainly it was not as reliable. So we -- by doing this, you combined the A, B, C, D, E, F, with the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. So if the judge told me something, that would probably be A1, particularly if it was -- if the other judges told me it as well; whereas if someone I had never met before who rushed up to me in the street and said something outrageous, might be F6, and it would be sort of one of those -- you know, a combination of those A to F and 1 to 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've obviously never heard of the appeal court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to remember that we didn't always have 15 lawyers at your elbow everywhere we went in Kosovo, sir. If only we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of my colleagues who were overturned -- sorry, who was affirmed in his decision by the appeals court when a friend commented on it said, Yes, but I still believe I'm right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And of course there is objectivity in this, but it was the best we could do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is this a standard way in analytical work to try to classify information this way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I mean, it is the standard way it's taught at staff colleges, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, the people who were doing the assessments of the events in Kosovo after the KVM had evacuated, they were the same staff members that had been in the fusion cell before; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. But they were also talking much more to our human rights people and drawing on the experience of the human rights people as well, because we were entering areas that we frankly haven't got a lot of experience of. And therefore, where there was expertise, we drew on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: For the record, first, I should just make clear that what with we have seen is Exhibit P407, page 945. We can remove it now from the ELMO. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the blue book, Exhibit 407, as an exhibit in its entirety at this point and as to the reason for doing this we submit that it's a one-stop shop which is very useful to have an overview of the events in Kosovo throughout the relevant period of time and, indeed, it's a document that has been referred to during cross-examination numerous times. So I think that it would be a handy document to have on record for everybody's reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the Defence would have an objection to the introduction on whole of everything in the blue book en masse, particularly given the testimony that's just been given at lines 12 through 15, that following the withdrawal of the KVM from Kosovo the persons compiling the blue book were talking more and more to the human rights people. That leads me to the belief that the -- that the matters that have been excluded from this trial already, namely the As Seen, As Told material, might now be finding its way in a much more controversial format into the blue book, to the extent that there might be some information flowing therefrom that is now replayed in the blue book. So that would be at least one basis for the objection on this -- on introducing this entire document into evidence without having foundation and basis for each of the points that are raised therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would join the submissions made by Mr. Ivetic and we would add that your order of 11 July 2006 on procedure and evidence, I can't cite the paragraph in that order, but therein the Chamber held that books of this -- large documents like this would not be admitted in total. Only those portions of these books which were actually put to witnesses would be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can -- maybe respond to that, those two submissions. With respect to the part of the blue book that concerns events after KVM had left Kosovo, we've just been through the general's evidence about how this evidence was assessed and you will see in relevant entries of the blue book how the system of rating the reliability of the evidence is being used based on this A through F and 1 through 6 system is used. So we would submit that it is entirely possible to assess the reliability of that and give appropriate weight to the entries in the blue book on that basis in the context of all the other evidence on record. And with respect to O'Sullivan's submission, I guess it might be a repetition, but we would submit that it is useful at this point to have a reference point on the record that can be referred to. And as I said, actually, this has been done on numerous occasions during cross-examination. So we would urge the admission of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your second argument simply means that the document has already been admitted so far as necessary, to understand the points that are being made in cross-examination; it doesn't really address the second matter of admitting this without exploration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just one question to clarify something for me. When I read this statement, I remember reading something about the UNHCR provision of material about the movement of refugees, I think. Can you recollect where in the statement that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do have the same recollection, if I can find it. I believe it's towards the end of the statement. Paragraph -- it might be paragraph 175 Your Honour is thinking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since we are in a state of ignorance about the contents of this book, we shall have a cursory look at it and give further consideration to the submissions that are being made, and we shall give you a decision tomorrow morning on this. I don't think that impedes your examination in any way, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I'll leave the topic of all these different documents, and I'd like to move to page 10 of your statement at paragraph 62, where you describe a meeting you had in Pristina on the 27th of November. What was the purpose of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We sat around the table in Pristina to work out how we were going to approach the meeting with the VJ General Staff in Belgrade. This was our first introductory meeting with the VJ General Staff, and it was important that we felt we had one chance to set the standard of what we expected from the VJ and therefore -- and because the KVM was comprised with people of different backgrounds and with different expectations, we sat down together to agree a joint position that we would go forward. This was not the way I would normally have done it in a military context, but this was not a military mission. And therefore, I was attempting to draw on all the expertise that there was and to make sure that it was not just -- it was not just my best guess, but it was using -- using the best guess and the knowledge and experience of those who I had available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And also that included Serb representatives. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The meeting in Pristina, no -- sorry, excuse me, yes. Sorry, I'm looking at 62 again. Sorry, there was first -- we had a -- we had a meeting first that was internal. Then from that we went and had this meeting, and at this meeting we attempted to -- to trail what we were expecting to achieve in the meeting in Belgrade. And the intention of sharing that was to try to avoid ambushing, surprising, senior people in the VJ. Because in my experience, it's always easier to deal with people if you don't walk into a meeting and immediately surprise them. So we felt it was important that they knew the sort of arguments we were going to bring forward, the sort of approach we were going to take, when we arrived in Belgrade. So it was an attempt to transparency and to try and set the stage for a successful meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I would like to take a look now at an exhibit, P2536, if we could call that up. And I guess we need a little zooming in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, we do. I really do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can we you see this or would you like us to move in a little further?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I know what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. And what are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We're looking at a document that was pasted into my working notebook, which - if I can explain - I always had a working notebook that I carried with me which would either have speaking notes that had been pre-prepared for me so that I made sure I didn't miss anything, or if I went into a meeting and I wasn't sure what the outcome was going to be I would at least take notes to remind myself later of what had been said and what hadn't been said and who was there to the best of my ability. So I tried to keep sort of a running record. And I think there are seven of these books, I'm afraid. But I also, if afterwards we produced a document that was particularly useful, then sometimes I would remember to glue it into the book and sometimes I wouldn't. This is the, as you see, the talking points that we agreed should be the basis of the conversation I had in Belgrade in the VJ Ministry of Defence, and it attempted to make it abundantly clear how we wanted to operate in order to carry out the mandate that had been given to the mission in the agreement that by that stage was over a month old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And these talking points, do they also reflect the information that was given in -- in Pristina to the Serb representatives there during the preparation meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was not given on paper, but it was -- it was described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like to then, if we could -- well, you then describe going to Belgrade and meeting with General Ojdanic. That's in paragraph 63. How would you describe the atmosphere at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was fairly neutral. It was not particularly friendly, but it was not hostile. It was less friendly than I would have wished, but not as hostile as it might have been. And because he had only very recently taken up his position, we knew that that meant we were going to get less out of the meeting because we knew that he would have had less time to be briefed and that he would be less inclined to make decisions at the meeting. And so we went into this meeting with lowered expectations, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And "he" is General Ojdanic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now if we could see Exhibit P2535, please. Again, we need zooming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document that was produced after the Belgrade meeting and was -- was to have been the speaking -- the basis for speaking notes with the Pristina Corps commander, because when I finished the meeting in Belgrade, the expectation was that I should then go on to have a subsequent meeting at the lower -- at the level below that, that is, with the commander on the ground. In the event that meeting did not take place and was cancelled at the -- on the orders, as I understand it, of Belgrade, but I had them all, I was all prepared for the meeting and they went into the book, and they actually served as a useful reminder of what had happened at the Belgrade meeting as well. And I think that's why they're valuable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- so -- but you left the meeting with General Ojdanic thinking that things had good sufficiently well to be able to follow up on this. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would say that I left the meeting with General Ojdanic feeling that there was the basis for -- for future cooperation. I didn't expect to be dealing with him on a day-to-day basis because he was sitting in Belgrade with other responsibilities than just Kosovo, obviously, and so what I wanted was to go to him to get him to issue an instruction to the Pristina Corps commander to deal direct with me. And then only to raise things to the level of the Belgrade Ministry of Defence if events proved impossible or too difficult down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P2543 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, this is the letter I wrote to General Ojdanic -- or at least I -- I drafted it. Now, I can't remember whether it actually went because at this stage there was -- were letters that were sent and letters that were drafted and not sent. I think this was sent, but as it was sent we were getting the message that we weren't going to be allowed to meet with the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would it help you if I indicate -- or if I told you that on the Serbian version that you signed, which is in e-court, there is a date of 2nd of December indicated; this would be the date of the letter. Do you think you would send the letter --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think we did send it. I think we sent it, and within a day we'd been told that the meeting was off, the meeting with the Pristina Corps commander was off, at the instructions of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So had a meeting been -- had steps been taken to actually set up a meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What steps had been taken?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: As I recall it, the meeting in Belgrade with General Ojdanic concluded with the -- me saying that my next step would be to go and meet the corps commander in Pristina, and I would be grateful if he could facilitate that and give orders to make sure that the meeting took place. I think we then proposed a date for a meeting, which was quite soon after the 27th of November because we were keen to get moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said that you were told that the meeting was called off. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I expect it was General Loncar. It was either -- it was -- excuse me. It either was General Loncar or the order came through General Loncar's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P418, please. And, Your Honours, this is an attachment to the witness statement that is DZ/9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, is this a record of the message you were given that the meeting was off, or is that talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think that's a separate thing. I think the message that the meeting with the corps commander was, at least, postponed came separately. But I recognise this and I'm aware of the context of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So if we first --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right. If we first deal, then, with the first communication calling off the meeting. What made you say that it was -- in Belgrade the decision had been taken not to have the meeting go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because my recollection was that the message that was given to me was that the meeting is off because the corps commander has been told that it's inappropriate for him to meet you, and that the -- the level of -- at which contact should be made should be through General Loncar's office and not direct to the Pristina Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you know who told the corps commander not to deal directly with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm then moving back to the exhibit that's on the screen here. What's the context of this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This was all happening at around about the same time. The original letter, the letter from Ambassador Walker to Mr. Milosevic was the thing that preceded my meeting in Belgrade, and this was a quite long letter which said, This is how we would propose to go about the verification process that has been called for in the -- in the agreement between the OSCE and FRY. That letter was never formally responded to but was -- we were rebuked over it because apparently we should not have sent it to Mr. Milosevic, we should have sent it to others in the government. But irrespective of that, there was never a formal response made to it by anybody. I then wrote my letter saying, This is how we propose to carry out inspections in a quite intrusive way, and this was to have been the basis of the meeting with the corps commander. And therefore, the second paragraph General Loncar picks up the inspections issue that I thought was an issue between me and the corps commander of the Pristina Corps but had been told, no, I was only to deal with General Loncar. And we were very keen to get started on inspections as soon as possible because we were under criticism for having been -- it was already at this stage six weeks since the mission had started to be stood up and people were saying, Okay, what are you doing? Can you hurry up, please, get started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You said the inspections were quite sort of intrusive. I can go back to the exhibit, but maybe can you just explain how -- what was it -- how did you foresee carrying out the inspections? What does it entail?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, because there was a need to confirm exactly what the level of -- in particular equipment, but equipment and manpower was on the ground, that needed to be checked. Now, it needed to be checked against a base-line, which we didn't have, and we wanted to check that the equipment was the same equipment, that equipment wasn't being moved in and out of Kosovo. And to do that, you weren't going to be able to do it by just standing at the roadside. You were going to have to do it by, for instance, going into every location, every military location in Kosovo at the same moment and counting the equipment all at the same moment so you did a one-time audit. That would be an intrusive inspection. And to make sure that it was done to the satisfaction of the OSCE in Vienna, we proposed to do it on a no-notice basis so that there was no -- so that we could prove that there was no possibility of collusion. And so by proposing a stringent inspection regime, we hoped to be able to prove that compliance was or was not taking place. We very much hoped that compliance was taking place, and the more collateral we could offer to show that compliance was taking place would assist everyone in calming the situation down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before moving to sort of the follow-up meeting with Sainovic that followed from this exhibit, I'd just like you to explain one thing for us. In paragraph 71 you talk about a medevac helicopter issue. What was that issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: In providing individuals as verifies for the Kosovo Verification Mission, the participating states of the OSCE expressed a lot of concern over the safety of the verifiers. It was a constant theme, particularly at the start. And this was very unhelpful because we wanted to get these verifiers as quickly as possible so we could get working, and remember there were 2.000 of them. And so what we needed to be able to demonstrate was that the verifiers were going to be safe in our hands. Part of that was the medical arrangements. Now, the medical arrangements in Kosovo, the state of the hospitals, was poor by western standards. There were much better facilities in Belgrade or in Macedonia, but within Kosovo there were very few -- there were really no medical facilities that we would wish to use. And to get this -- to get this view of it, I had a medical expert lent to me by the UK as part of the -- one of the early verifiers. And so we -- we were quite clear that we didn't want to use the local medical facilities if we would possibly avoid it. And also, if we had been using the local medical facilities, it was inevitable that we would have gone to the head of the queue in any situation and that would have rebounded in a bad way, that we were demanding priority treatment over locals, and therefore we wanted to provide self-standing medical cover. This was debated a lot up in Vienna, and as a result the Permanent Council required the secretariat to do something about it quickly. And as a result of that, they hired a Swiss medevac helicopter which was fully equipped and had a doctor and life-support assistance on the machine, and having hired it they then told us and said, Here you are, we've got one of these for you. And we said, Great, that's just what we want but we'd better make sure that we can bring it in. And so at that point we asked Bo Pellnas who was our liaison man in Belgrade to get authority to fly the helicopter in. And we felt certainly at the start that this was a mere formality, because ability to use air corridors and landing at airports was specifically mentioned in the original agreement between the OSCE and the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did it become an issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It became an issue because we did not get the clearance to bring it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you told why you weren't given clearance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The issue was raised within Belgrade, and the information that I received was that this was on the desk of Mr. Sainovic, and that Mr. Sainovic would say yes or no. To start with, we were asked, What are the exact technical specifications of the helicopter? And we gave those. And still, we didn't get the all-clear. There was at some stage an offer by the Serbs to make available military medical evacuation helicopters, and we did not want those, partly because they were obviously identifiable as Serb assets and we were going to be flying -- we would be flying around Kosovo with Albanians on the ground with guns. And they didn't -- they wouldn't have known that there was an international on a stretcher in them. So we felt that that contained an element of danger. And the other thing was that they were not of the same -- equipped to the same standard, not anything like the same standard that the medevac helicopter was that we had already contracted. And so for both those reasons, we wanted to stick with ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did it have any implication for the KVM that you were not allowed to have the medevac helicopter?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, the whole drawn-out process became a litmus test of cooperation between the Yugoslav authorities and ourselves, and so it assumed a proportion perhaps out of size to its importance. I mean, it was important, but it became an issue which was described as, This is the first time we've come to you for something really specific, this appears to be an absolutely clear-cut case, ability to bring in things by air and to use airspace is specifically mentioned. It was specifically mentioned that this would be provided it was deemed to be necessary by the head of mission, the head of mission personally said, I deem this to be necessary, and yet we got nowhere on it. So we felt it was inexplicable that the level of cooperation was so low. And we were frankly amazed by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll jump now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I before -- may I ask before you do that. What facility was ultimately used for medical treatment or attention necessary to OSCE staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got together a number of ambulances supplied by one of the sending countries with paramedics permanently attached, so that each regional centre had, I think, two ambulances with professional paramedics available to it. And when we were -- when we suffered casualties, that was the way we got them out and obviously it took a lot longer than helicopter evacuation would have done. And again, we were not assisted in the way we got our people out at that stage because it's perhaps worth remarking that having suffered casualties and with two injured people in the back of these vehicles, they got to the -- the border with Macedonia and were all set to drive over the border with Macedonia. And the official -- the Serbian border official very helpfully said, Of course, if any of you guys going over the -- going over the border have single-entry visas, then you won't be coming back, will you, until you've got another visa from Belgrade, which will take several weeks. Now, this was our medical cover for all of us. And so at that stage we had to strap up the injured individuals who had to walk the 150 yards or so that existed between the Serbian border post and the Macedonian border post in order to get into the ambulance that was waiting for them that NATO had provided from its assets. That was particularly unhelpful, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, moving back now to -- to the chronology. In paragraph 80 -- well, 81, rather, you describe a meeting at the Pellumbi restaurant.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In which Walker, yourself, Sainovic, and Loncar participated.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, again, what was the atmosphere like at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We went -- the international -- the OSCE part of this meeting went into this meeting thinking it was going to be a negotiation session. We knew what the current issues were that we felt were needing resolution, and we expected to come out of that meeting with resolution on at least some of them and some -- some indication of the degree of cooperation we were going to receive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did it go that way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, it didn't. It didn't go a bit that way, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How did the meeting begin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact order of the meeting, but I think quite early on Mr. Sainovic berated the head of mission, Ambassador Walker, on the support that was being given to the Kosovo Liberation Army through the western banking system, and specifically from America, and demanding that Walker relay back to his authorities that the western banking system was to cease carrying the money which was, I think, in some cases remittances from European countries to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, General, if I can just interrupt you there. Did the KVM have any mandate or anything that would make banking relevant to your mission?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. I mean, it was above our pay grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you -- so I guess the meeting didn't start off too well. And then you say that all your requests were rejected, all the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me. It seems to me that in regard of these critical parts of the statement of the witness, the question should not be leading; rather, the question should be put as if this were viva voce testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Well, your question says: "You say all your requests were rejected." Where does he say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At paragraph 81. "Sainovic read a list of complaints and rejected all KVM requests" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very well. Yes, there's nothing leading about the question. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so what were the KVM requests?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, it took, it happened the other way in -- when I think Walker brought up the issue of the medical helicopter, which we heard had became a sort of cause celebre by this stage, Mr. Sainovic responded and said, Well, there's no way you're getting that, or you're certainly not getting that, and while we are on the subject, there are going to be no intrusive inspections, and we are certainly not going to reduce the police presence in a particular area called Malisevo, and we don't propose to set up a specific office in Pristina to expedite the issue of visas. Those, I recall, were the specific things. So it wasn't sort of a question and answer; it was a statement that picked up everything by Mr. Sainovic and left us with pretty much no more requests because he'd covered them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We've already talked about -- touched upon the visa issue and the medevac issue. Could you explain, what was the issue about Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Malisevo was an area to the west that had been the scene of particularly heavy fighting and was pretty much in the centre of the area where the KLA were active. The village was entirely Albanian. There was a police station in it, which was heavily fortified, and the behaviour of the policemen, we felt, having observed it, was making the situation worse not better. And therefore, what we had said was, Look, we're prepared to put our people on the ground in Malisevo in order to talk to the police, to talk to the local mayor, to try to reduce the level of tension here. But you've got to help as well because we believe the police in this case are part of the problem. And so we'll put people in, provided you agree that you're going to reduce the posture and the number of police in that police station, which was a fortified outpost. It was not -- it was not a community police station; it was a fort with armoured vehicles and so on. And this was, as I say, in the context of it being really an area where there was a continued standoff between the Albanian population and the police. And the police -- no, I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was it about the conduct of the police that the KVM felt was creating tension?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was the general aggressive way in which they operated and dealt with the Kosovar Albanian people in general, but it was -- it was particularly bad in this area. It was -- it had the appearance of an -- an occupying garrison rather than the forces of law and order of a sovereign state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To help the Court appreciate the situation, are there any specific examples of conduct that you could mention so we can understand the nature of this tension?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I would say that the -- the way the police dealt with the Kosovar Albanians was -- was not in a way that was -- that would endear them. They were very, very rough with them. They frequently stopped them and searched them at check-points, stopped buses and made everybody get out of the bus and searched them, not just males but women and children. It was a policy of generally harassing -- no, I don't know whether it was a policy, but the result we saw on the ground was that it was almost impossible for a Kosovar Albanian to go from A to B without being stopped and harassed by the Serb police on several occasions and that this aggressive approach was particularly bad the further west you went. And Malisevo was one particular area where they -- the police didn't go from the -- move out of their police station except to drive around in armoured vehicles and basically force anyone off the road who got in their way. This was not community policing as we know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I understand that from what the KVM observed the same kind of conduct also took place in other parts of Kosovo, although on a lesser scale. Would that be a correct understanding of the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It was particularly pronounced in Malisevo, which was why there was something of a standoff there, that we were attempting to reduce the level of tension because it was symbolic. We didn't have enough people to be everywhere. So what we wanted was to put some people into specific areas where we could see the problem was worse to try to achieve something which could be publicised to the benefit of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In these kind of incidents of harassment, how frequent were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, very frequent. I mean, I would expect that on a day as I drove around I would see Kosovar Albanians being -- being stopped at check-points at least once a day, and the -- I mean, it was almost so commonplace that it didn't get reported enough because we became used to the fact that it was going on. It was background activity. It was -- we didn't really have enough paper to report all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I guess I should start thinking about the time. Towards the end of paragraph 81 you say that Loncar grimaced. What did you make of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I felt that Loncar was uncomfortable with the way the meeting had developed. I didn't get the impression that he went into that meeting expecting to have the -- the verbal fight between Walker and Sainovic that took place. I think the pair of them wound each other up to a degree, and the result was more unfortunate than Loncar had expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll jump to some other issues in your statement now. In paragraph 87, you describe the ambush of the resupply convoy of the KLA. Did -- did KVM report on this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was it reported as a breach of the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, as a major breach of the cease-fire agreement by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now -- then I'd like to move on to the Podujevo training part of your statement, paragraph 94, 95, and the subsequent paragraphs. At paragraph -- well, I guess we'll just go to -- Paragraph 94, you say that you considered the manoeuvres to be provocative. Why were they provoking, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was described to us as driver training. And the reason -- the way it came about was Colonel -- General Loncar and Colonel Kotur saying that, We've got all these conscripts, they have to be trained. One of the things they've got to be trained in is driving tanks, so they need to do tank driver training. And we said, Okay, got that. Said, So we need to put them on to a training area. So we said, Okay, where is the training area? And there was a sort of -- Over here. We said, Well, that's not a training area. Training areas are where you have a specific area on a map that has boards when you going into it, and it says you're entering a training area, and everybody knows where it is. And the reply was, No, no, no, what we do is we go out and we always drive around here, and it's just what we always do. So it was, in effect, driving over private land. And I said, Well, given where we know the KLA are, if you drive tanks past some of these villages, it's highly likely that somebody's going to take offence at that and interpret it as -- as tanks coming after them. And if then somebody fires out of that village and you fire back into the village, then you've got an incident that doesn't need to happen, and therefore, if you need to do that, why not do it in an area where you're not going to go within a hundred metres of villages, where we know that the -- that there is KLA sympathy. Do it somewhere else and we can understand it, but please don't do it in an area where you are bound to provoke a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did the training actually provoke a response, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did the VJ respond once being fired on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, on being fired at they exercised their right of self-defence and they fired back, and therefore they fired into the villages from which fire had come with, first, machine-gun fire and then with tank main armament in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, had there been any firing exercises included in the -- in the training programme, as it was described to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, it was described as driver training. But -- I mean, I'm -- I understand that -- if I'd been in charge of VJ soldiers in Kosovo at the time, I would -- and I was going to deploy tanks, I would certainly have made sure the tanks had ammunition with them. It would have been stupid not to. So the fact that they had ammunition was not in question. I think all of the tanks were bombed up with ammunition all the time, and I would have been surprised if they weren't. But they -- their ability to return fire was the issue that I was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The detail of this I don't think is in the statement, is it, the actual exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came later, sir. It developed over days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But was there one particular event where fire was exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember reporting it back to Walker, because I remember Walker going in front of the media and using a phrase that, In our view, they went looking for trouble and they found trouble. And I remember that phrase very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where and when this was or is that something that's simply noted somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- it would have been in the -- say, the third week of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the -- in the villages in the area of Podujevo, which is about 30 minutes' drive north of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that there were exchanges of fire in more than one village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe I should at this stage alert Your Honours to the fact that I have maybe another hour or so to go, although I think I might have used more than two hours. So I might be going a little over time. I will seek your leave to do that. We had indicated three hours, but I hope the evidence is helpful and that it's warranted to go through this in some detail, but otherwise I can cut it short. I can also do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't see a problem about you taking, within reason, what time is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I shall try to keep a reasonable momentum. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we can move on to paragraph 103, that is a paragraph that begins at the top of page 16. You describe having a meeting with Lukic on the 24th of December. Now, I'd like to show you Exhibit P2544.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I've got nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think there something's come up.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, from this view do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. This would have been a note of the meeting taken by the young man that I took with me to do precisely that, to take the note to make sure we had a record of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: David Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, here the Malisevo incident was discussed in paragraph 2. In paragraph 4, you express concern about excessive use of force, and you talk about the Podujevo incident.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you expressed these concerns. What was General Lukic's response to this? Did you feel it sort of resonated with him in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. He -- he was quite defensive -- well, he did not agree with me that this was -- this was inappropriate activity. He made the point very strongly that the safety of his policemen was paramount to him, which I -- which I understood and certainly sympathised with. But my point was made strongly that going about his policing activities in this way was making the situation more inflamed, not less inflamed. And this was in the context of increasing instances of heavy-handed policing throughout the area, but particularly starting to happen up in -- in the Podujevo area, which was an area where it hadn't been to the same degree earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we move down to the -- to the bottom of the page in your statement we just talked about, paragraph -- page 16. At paragraphs 109 and 110, you describe an incident - and 111, I'm sorry - you describe an operation to recover the body of a Serb -- an elderly Serb man that had been shot.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I understand the debate basically was how to carry this out. On the one hand, you describe Walker being of the view that this should be done as a rather low-key operation and there was a proposal by Loncar to use a number of heavy vehicles and I guess a number of MUPs in this operation -- MUP staff in this operation. Why -- why did Walker propose this low-key operation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because every time -- this was an area where the Kosovo Liberation Army had become very clear that it was starting to operate there. We were still attempting to get them to step back, and there was no way we were going to get them to step back if large numbers of police in armoured vehicles turned up and, in effect, aggravated the situation. So our point was that we can -- we can do our best to talk the situation down, to talk to the Kosovo Liberation Army to get them to step back, because they were certainly occupying positions that -- they were moving into positions they had not been before. So they were being aggressive, and we understood that, but we felt the way that -- to get them to step back was not to flood the area with police in armoured vehicles. The point then was then made that here is someone who sadly has been killed. We need to get his body out. We said, Okay, we'll help you get the body out, but let's do it in a non-confrontational way so that in getting one body out we don't create the circumstances in which more bodies -- more dead bodies are created. And that was the whole basis of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why that proposal, that is Walker's proposal, was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly -- it was changing the parameters that we were operating on, that my mission was operating on, because we were, in effect, offering to do a job for the police which was extending our mandate to a degree. We were -- I mean, we were asking the police to lower their profile, and in return for them lowering their profile, we would help them. So it was -- yeah, I mean, it was a negotiation but it was a genuine offer to try to keep the level of violence down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This may tie in with something else. I'd like you -- if you could go to page 19 of your statement, paragraph 134. In the last part of that paragraph you say: "From my observation and with the benefit of my military training, it is my opinion that the Serbian military strategy, when trying to combat the insurgency (KLA), was very poor."

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why -- why do you think that, why was the strategy poor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because it was clearly not working. They were alienating or they had alienated the Kosovar Albanian population to the degree there was more -- there was a greater tendency in the Kosovar Albanian population to support and to give support to the KLA. There was no real attempt made by the Serbian authorities to expose the criminal activities of the KLA when they took place. There was no attempt to find evidence, arrest members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, put them on trial, find them guilty, and send them to jail for a long time, which is -- there was no real information campaign by the Serbian government to -- to change the way that the incidents were seen down in Kosovo. So it was all reaction and overreaction and no attempt to put it into context and no attempt to talk-up the genuine position that the Serbian authorities had, which was that they were the sovereign power there, which we understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How about the military strategy be used, do you think that was effective?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. Because -- I mean, my -- I think the recurring theme that came into all of my -- so many of my conversations with the -- with Serbian authorities was of provocative behaviour of disproportionate use of force, that if you have a village where Kosovar Albanians live and they are giving tacit support to the Kosovo Liberation Army, the way to win them over is not to flatten the village with artillery. The way to win them over is to persuade them that -- of the benefits of supporting the powers that be, whether it's by -- by dealing with them in a more sensitive way or by making sure electricity is connected, by making sure that if someone is arrested that they go through due process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And from a tactical point of view, do you think the forces of the FRY and Serbia could have achieved better results had they carried out their operations in a different way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What should they have done?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, they were the best recruiting sergeant for the KLA that there was. Because once they had fired into villages with heavy weapons, the KLA would creep back and say, There you are, that's what you get from the people who are supposed to be the forces of law and order. And so -- I mean, to operate differently would have required a completely different strategy that would have needed to have been promulgated to everybody. It would have needed extensive re-training of the individuals on the ground. It could not have been done overnight, but you could not have mistaken it if there had been a different approach because that different approach would have had to have been described by senior Serbian politicians. And then when policemen or soldiers overstepped the mark, then there would have been investigations, there would have been consequences, which we never saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you discuss your views on different ways of doing things with any of your Serbian liaisons or interlocutories?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. It was a constant theme of my conversations with -- my meetings with General Loncar and his staff, and people like Colonel Kotur, Colonel Mijatovic, who were present at many of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your estimate, how many fighting men did the KLA have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Several hundred that were actually full-time fighters sitting on the top of the hills. Then the villages had people that were prepared to turn out to defend their village if their village was attacked, but they weren't sort of KLA fighters; they were KLA auxiliaries, I would say. But they were not available for anything that didn't involve their own village. We saw instances of villages being assaulted by Serb forces, where the next village over our people would go along and be talking to the head man of the village and saying, Well, over that hill 3 miles away, you know, there's a fight going on. And the head man would say, Yes, and we're going to sit here and do nothing about it because it's nothing to do with us. And so there was not a sort of call to arms and everybody rush towards the fight. And so several hundred would have been my estimate of KLA strength on the ground in Kosovo around about December/January of 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you think the Serb forces could have dealt with this KLA force had they used different tactics?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What tactics should they have used in your view to do this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, they needed to -- they needed to make it clear that the average Kosovar Albanian had nothing to fear from the Serb forces. Now, to do that, they needed to show that by the way they -- the way they dealt with them. And that would have required a clear decision by the regime to go about it in a different way. I mean, it's a completely different way of doing things. I mean, we would call it a hearts and minds campaign, but it's actually re-establishing the legitimacy of the forces of that sovereign state, making sure the police did what police are supposed to do, which is to protect the inhabitants of the country, not to harass them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to Racak and I just want to be sure I'm not getting into something I shouldn't. No, this should be safe. Paragraph 156, if you would look at that, that is on page 22.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, the paragraph mentioned by Mr. Marcussen, 156, can be seen as temporarily redacted pursuant to your earlier decision. What was mentioned here was - and I may be corrected if I'm wrong - from paragraphs 154 up to 157, included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think you've been -- it may be a bad translation. It was 147 to 154. Now, I hope that will be rectified if it's been wrongly translated for you. You've got all the right numbers but not in the right order.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, to your knowledge, on the 16th had there been an attempt by the investigating judge to enter Racak and carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, but I personally didn't witness it. But yes, I -- from what she told me the next day, I understood she had attempted to go in on the 16th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what had happened, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: She had gone in with a police -- a large police escort and they had been fired on from the vicinity of the village and so had withdrawn without getting to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so you describe that later on you discussed with Judge Marinkovic the possibility of entering the village again.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Judge Marinkovic proposed essentially to use the same method as she had already tried before, to go back into Racak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then you describe how she went in and actually did draw fire also during that later attempt. Have you any view as to why Judge Marinkovic preferred to use the MUP option than the KVM option?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, she was a very determined lady and had a very firm view of her responsibilities as the investigating judge and -- I mean, I -- she may have been right. My point that I was making to her over several hours in -- in quite heated circumstances was that what we were trying to avoid was to flare up the situation anymore, and that I understood fully that it was her job to get in and establish the cause of death of the people that were by the -- whose bodies at that stage were in the mosque in Racak, but we could help her do that without causing the fighting to flare up again, if she would just allow us to help her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there actually someone in her company killed in -- as a result of the fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. When she went in this time on I think the Sunday afternoon, it ended up with one of the policemen being killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we need to interrupt shortly, Mr. Marcussen. Is this convenient or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me have one -- if Your Honours allow one question relating to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- and then we'll be finished with Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At paragraph 180 of your statement, which is at page 25, the second-last paragraph, you mention this situation where Judge Marinkovic goes into Racak with the MUP as an example of MUP-VJ coordination.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain that. She's going in with the MUP. Were there any VJ involved as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there were any VJ involved in the place where I was with her. It was a police station and everybody I could see was in the police. The point was that from the moment she said, Right, we're going in, it happened quite quickly. And for that to happen implied, implied very firmly, that there was someone that she was talking to who was in charge of the entire situation because the set-up was that the -- the VJ were on the hills and ridges overwatching the area, giving cover to the police that were going to go in. Now, to do that and to know when to open fire and when not to open fire, there's got to be someone in charge. You can't do that by having a vague sort of relationship. There's got to be someone who says, Cease fire now or don't -- or open fire now, otherwise people get killed. I mean, it's what coordination is about. So you couldn't possibly have said, Okay, we're going in and do it quickly, unless there was an existing state of command arrangement over the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And on that day, to your knowledge, did the VJ open fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say that the VJ were on the hills and ridges overwatching the area, giving cover to the police that were going in, you're talking of overwatching the area of the village of Racak, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you see VJ on the hills and ridges overwatching the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This may be a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now need to break for lunch, Mr. Drewienkiewicz. If you could withdraw again with the usher, we'll see you again at 1.45 -- in fact, at 1.50, I think, just to give the full hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we shall resume at 1.50. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I very briefly add to the discussion regarding the blue book P407 this morning, having done some additional research?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just very quickly, it was suggested that because of this rating system that it took on some authority that it otherwise might not have, especially toward the end. Let me give you an example. At page 943 they talk about reports from unnamed people that they saw dead bodies and they call that fairly reliable and complies with behaviour patterns so therefore possibly true. Now, there's no basis for that kind of thing. Another one, and it has conclusions, the abduction of Albanian males of fighting age is most likely a gambit by Serb forces to prevent the men from joining the KLA. Now there is simply no evidence that would come even close to supporting that in this case, and I don't think there will be. So I really don't think this is a reliable document, and I think you ought to very strictly apply your order on procedure and evidence, paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In spite of Mr. Ackerman's desire to have the last word, you're entitled to it, Mr. Marcussen, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, fearing it can be an even longer afternoon I'll have one crack at it. Now I think the issues that Mr. Ackerman pointed out, I mean, these sort of things go to weight, and it can be seen from the document itself what kind of information the report is based on in the different parts and that is exactly why we say it could be admitted because it is plausible to assess the information and the basis in the report based on the report itself, so it should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as I said earlier, we'll consider the position and tell you tomorrow morning. So you can carry on now with the examination of Mr. Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you -- I guess we have partly covered this, but I will just make sure that we've fully covered this issue. If you wouldn't mind looking at paragraph 164 of your statement; that is on page 23.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You describe -- we've already touched upon why it is that you thought that the Podujevo operation and what was going on there was provocation. But what do you mean when you say that the situation was horrible? What was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think I would say that this is where -- this is my state of mind in January, and maybe what was -- what I thought was horrible in January was more commonplace later. So this was -- this was a younger me looking at this. But it was -- the situation around Podujevo was that complete hamlets were being depopulated and the inhabitants were being driven from them, simply to deny the possibility of there being anybody in there that could be -- could be seen as being a civilian as opposed to a fighter, and all of -- it was widely reported in the media at the time, and so this situation was being well publicised internationally. And the whole thing was serving to escalate the situation in a way that was not helpful to anybody in my view. And I just felt it was the wrong way to be doing this, that a lot of it was tit for tat; in other words, one side would do something which would be responded to by the other side to a greater degree and the other side would come back, and somebody had to break the cycle of violence, and this was my view at the time. And the situation in which we were having to appeal to everybody to let us get through to move wounded people around, to extract corpses, this was not what we had been sent down there to do. This was not what we had felt the government of -- of the federal republic wanted us to do. We just -- I just thought that it needed -- people needed to look at it from how it was seen from the outside rather than in the context of day-to-day provocation and to realise the damage that it was doing to the whole process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, moving again on to something else. In paragraph 167, you -- well, beginning at 165 and then 166, 167, you talk about the incident at Rogovo, and I believe you were there yourself to see the scene.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I showed it earlier but I would like to again call up Exhibit P673, please. And I think you already commented that you were familiar with this report because you were at Rogovo yourself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What I would like to show you is page 3 of the document, please. Yeah, if we can scroll a little more up. Here is a list of victims and sort of a brief description of how the scene looked. Does that look correct to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, that 20-something, yes, yes, and one dead Serb policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Serb -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, this is one of the documents I mentioned earlier that we would like to tender then. The specific part we are relying on is the description of how things looked at Rogovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you something else about a related document if we could call up P646 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Oh, I see my learned friend is on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to draw your attention to the toponym being Rogovo, R-o-g-o-v-o. Rugova is another toponym, another place name, just so that we can avoid any further clarification [as interpreted]. Perhaps we can have it clarified in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It should be Rogovo, of course. I was going to ask you just one rather minor question about what are described as a group of policemen wearing light grey coveralls. What is a coverall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like a boiler suit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Like an overall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. No, that's all I wanted to know. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me see if we have -- right. So this exhibit is an attachment to the general's statement. Now maybe I should ask -- my admission earlier, when I requested that the general's statement be admitted, I was sort of thinking that along with it went all the attachments to the statement, but it might not be so obvious as they have actually been given separate exhibit numbers. So I just wanted to clarify this, my request that the statement plus the related attachments be admitted, and that is one of the attachments we are now -- to clarify that point. I can give the exhibit numbers so -- for easy reference. The attachments have P73, P418, P616, P634 to P641, then there's a gap, and then we have P643 to P651.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any objection to following that course? No. Very well. We'll admit these as part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we go to the next page of this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just one thing for clarification. There are a number of asterisks in the document at different of places. Do you know why that is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because the words couldn't be deciphered from these -- the handwritten scrawl of the young man that was taking notes for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then I ask if we could go to the next page, please. And could we zoom down -- could we zoom in just at the last part which says: "DZ, I'm not going to mention Racak," and that part here. Well, I guess the sensitivity of Racak is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But then you say: "So can I confirm that you agree to a joint investigation?" And General Loncar responds: "Yes, absolutely." Was a joint investigation ever carried out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would it have been possible to carry out a joint investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We were desperate for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your view, was a proper investigation carried out where you, KVM, was involved in it, but was a proper investigation carried out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. It absolutely was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because it was all over so quickly. The investigating magistrate was in and out of the scene of crime within about two hours, and this was a huge area, ankle-deep in mud and water and slush, in which there had been a very major exchange of fire and 20-something people had been killed. It would have taken days to have worked out -- taken all the evidence from that scene of crime if a proper investigation had been carried out. And it would have involved probably draining the area to find out where all the bullet -- spent bullets were, where the bullets had gone to. It would have involved a proper forensic examination of the dead. None of that was carried out at all. It could not possibly have been carried out in two hours by one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What would be the appropriate action to take when you come across armed KLA groups like this and you are the forces of law and order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would engage them -- well, you might invite them to surrender, but assuming they don't you would certainly engage them. And I would expect that there would be a fire-fight if they were all KLA, and anyone who was innocent would immediately make it clear that he was not part of this and would probably surrender. And after a brief exchange of fire, a number of them, the ones that resisted, would have been injured and down, and the remainder would be standing there with their hands in the air. And at that point, they are then taken away and charged. What was astonishing was that everybody was dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 174 of your statement and also then again later on towards the end, I think it's paragraph 208, you touch on the issue of whether or not there was a pre-existing master plan to expel the Albanian population from Kosovo. Could there have been a plan that you did not know about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- I'm sorry. That question just absolutely calls for pure speculation. That couldn't possibly -- the answer could not possibly be evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marcussen, what was the reason for this question, bearing in mind that I think it's already been answered in a different way to the effect that the witness didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, I -- all I was getting at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I could have given you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If that is clear to everyone that that's the position, then I don't need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we can move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Paragraph 176 you talk about touring the border zone with Kotur and I guess other people. Why were you in the border zone with Kotur?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This -- this was while Rambouillet was on, and there was a number of discussions that were going on at Rambouillet, and one was about how in any future settlement the border zone was to be kept secure. And there was some proposals floating around Rambouillet that suggested that the border zone was somehow something that could be policed very easily. And I was not convinced that this was the case because I knew it to be very rugged country. And in that context, as well as needing to get out and see what was happening generally, I agreed that I would go around the area west of Prizren with Colonel Kotur and he would show me what it looked like, to confirm what I indeed was pretty sure of, that this was not an area that could be -- that could be policed by a few gendarmarie, that if you wanted to seal this border it was going to be -- going to require a very significant effort, which in turn would translate into a very significant police or army presence, which was the thing that was being discussed at Rambouillet at the time. So that was the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were there, to your knowledge, at Rambouillet any considerations given to limiting the number of VJ or MUP that could be in the border zone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. And the number that was -- the numbers that were being talked about were simply unrealistic and at the request of the folk in Rambouillet, we did a calculation of what we thought would be a reasonable force to carry out surveillance of this border zone, firstly with and then without electronic means. And this was important because at the time Serbia had no access to electronic means, which would have made their life easier in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that the proposals coming from the internationals involved in the negotiations were unrealistically low?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you offer to the Serb authorities to make an assessment or did they ask you or how did it come about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We made an assessment -- we made an assessment. I asked the Serbs to help me go and look at this area, so that I could provide the most credible assessment to the international community in Rambouillet because they had already asked me to provide an assessment. And I said, Well, I would like to go and look at it on the ground, and then I'll make the assessment, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you an attachment to your statement DZ7, and that is P640, if we would be able to call that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could go to the second page of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, can you see this or do we need to zoom --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yeah, that looks very -- very familiar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are kindly asking the speakers to make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I point out that the date of the 21st of June, 2000 is the date that the particularly complicated machine I had at the time printed it off, not the date that it was initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When about is this document from; do you think?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was from mid-February because that's when we looked at this. So this is the product of the visit to the border with Colonel Kotur and some thought after it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you remember how many personnel the Serb authorities thought were needed to guard the border?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I seem to remember it was in the order of -- it was several thousand, I mean at least 5.000, and possibly more, and my inclination was to broadly agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe we could just see the second page of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Which I think confirms paragraph 9, the VJ estimated 6 to 7.000 people being needed, and KVM coming to something in the same order in paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
