utterances.text: Now, you also describe -- you describe -- you describe Kotur exposing contempt for the Albanians in Kosovo. Was there anything else that happened that day that gave you this impression of contempt being exposed by Kotur?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. We went into one of the villages on -- up against the border, about 2 kilometres from the border, and we all arrived in the village and we were about eight vehicles, probably, so we were something of an event. The head man of the village, who was a Kosovar Albanian, was called for. He was not present, so the next in seniority appeared, and we all moved into the meeting house of the village. In moving into the meeting house, I started to take -- remove my boots, as I understand to be the custom, and Colonel Kotur said, You really don't need to do that, you know. And I said, Well, where I come from, this is what you do. And so I told my people to make sure they took off their boots and went into the meeting house in stocking feet and sat around the wall as -- as is the custom. Colonel Kotur went into the meeting house in his boots, and instead of sitting down on the floor, demanded that a chair be brought for him on which he then sat with the -- the senior Kosovar Albanian squatting on his haunches at the -- at the foot of the chair rather like a medieval peasant, and I thought it was a particularly unfortunate way of dealing with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And remarked so. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you remember the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I could find it from my copious notes, but not off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to move -- jump again, and this time I'm jumping to the end of paragraph 181 at the top of page 26. There you use the expression "blue on blue." "Otherwise there's a strong risk of 'blue on blue' contact." What is blue-on-blue contact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Traditionally on our tactical maps friendly forces were depicted in blue and enemy forces in red. And so if you shoot at and hit your own troops, that's a blue-on-blue contact, and obviously it's to be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so you are explaining in this part of your statement that you think there would have been coordination between the MUP and the VJ because otherwise there was a risk of basically Serb forces firing on themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. Particularly because there were very disparate levels of training involved here and of course the VJ consisted on conscripts who are generally less well-trained than professional troops, and therefore it's very important that you have very, very unambiguous rules when you're using conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, how about if you use reserve forces or maybe local police or something like that, how would you avoid blue-on-blue -- that kind of a scenario?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, you -- the less well trained and -- people are and the less good communications they've got, the less strong chain of command they've got, the more risk you introduce into these incidents. The best way of doing it is not to have any of those and to stick to your regulars. And every time you bring in others of these elements, you -- you introduce risk which you can only get rid of by lengthy briefings and putting people into a position and saying, Right, don't move from here. This is your left of arc, this is your right of arc, if anything moves outside of there, under no circumstances do you open fire and don't do anything until I tell you. And if somebody says, Stop, for God's sake stop. It's got to be really simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 190 you describe seeing some MUP units seemed to be more motived, fitter, sort of more professional unit. Now, did you ever learn the name of these units?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, I'd like if we could see Exhibit P2538.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think if we could go to page 4. I think I'd like to the usher to assist us also with the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, this is a picture I believe you provided to us. It comes from a publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would like the ELMO to be turned on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, do you have the original of the publication?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe we could place that on the ELMO. What I propose we do, Your Honours, is in due course we replace the page that is shown now in e-court with a colour scan of what is being shown on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, you're referring sometimes to a webbing. Is that something we can see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. That's the web equipment around the body of the policeman with the helmet on, and indeed on the body of the policeman with the hat on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did the policemen that you saw that day, did they look like these two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They had similar webbing. They were wearing camouflage green uniforms, not dark blue, and they looked a darn sight smarter than this pair. They were shaven and their bearing was what I would call more upright and alert. So this picture I think is at Malisevo in about December or January. But the webbing is the same sort of webbing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We are done with the ELMO for now. We will need it in a bit for another page in that. You can leave the thing there. We will get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At paragraph 188, so two paragraphs back, you say that at least one new VJ unit came into Kosovo on the 16th of March. How do you know that it was not just some new T-72 tanks that came in but actually a unit?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Because the T-72 is a completely different tank to the T-55, which was the -- all of the tanks in Kosovo were T-55s. This is an older tank with a different set of duties for each crew member, and the T-72 is a completely different tank to operate. And so you couldn't take the existing crew, a T-55, and tell them to jump into a T-72 and operate it. Many things in the way you operate that tank are completely different. For instance, the number of people in the crew is different, and so the duties of each crew member are different. And of course when you're dealing with conscripts, you train them on one specific piece of equipment because that's all you have time to do. And so the idea of replacing T-72s by T-55s as though you were slipping out of a pair of brown shoes into a pair of black shoes with conscripts is very difficult for me to comprehend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was it a violation of existing agreements to introduce a new unit, a new armoured unit like this on the 16th of March?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, because the -- the original agreement going back to October of 1998 had required that the units in Kosovo be at the level that they'd been at in the spring of 1998. And the arms control declaration, which we had legitimately, for the -- for the area of Kosovo showed that the only tanks there were T-55. There were no T-72s declared under the arms control -- the various arms control agreements inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the base-line also include the figures for the number of tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At this period in time, so around the middle of March, 16th of March, was it your view that the situation had changed and that international agreements were not so important anymore?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, because it would have been possible and indeed may well have taken place that a unit that did not have such recognisable equipment could have been added into Kosovo and we might not have known. But to see such highly recognisable different equipment as a T-72 was something that could not be -- could not be hidden, and it was recognised as such and attention was drawn to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit P2533, please. Can you see this on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This looks like my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember making this entry, or is it actually your entry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it's a note to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's a note to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: And I'm sure it's out of my -- out of one of my notebooks. It's probably out of notebook 6 if we are being specific, and it would have -- by saying it was 8.00, it was almost certainly made during the 8.00 meeting that we had with Walker and Keller and all the other deputy heads around the table at which we exchanged views and concluded what the situation of the mission was. So this would be a mix of the notes that I made for myself to give to the other members and the conclusions that were reached around the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And around the middle of the page you say "distinct change of Belgrade attitude." And then you list three points.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Does that reflect your recollection of the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, the fact that they might have slipped units in with the same equipment as everybody else and we might not have noticed, so they're no longer reinforcing by stealth, which we suspected, but they are now reinforcing overtly and the fact that the change to the border zone refers to an official decision emanating from Belgrade to widen the border zone from 5 kilometres to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And then at the bottom of your -- of the page, you have a note saying that there were 10.000 internally displaced persons in Mitrovica. Was that something that was created around that time, the 17th of March, or was it something that had happened earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That -- well, if you look, you see we've now gone to 9.00, so that would have been the next meeting. And that would have come out of the briefings that were given to all of us at that stage. And the fact that they're now reporting 10.000 internally displaced people is seen as the current situation, which would have been different to that days and weeks earlier because it was a particular bone of contention within the international community how many people were displaced, were on the road. And it was an issue of some discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why was it difficult -- well, was it difficult to find out how many internally displaced persons there were?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: There were a lot of different reports, and we were not keen to -- to give veracity to reports that we could not see on the ground. And we at this stage generally found it difficult to find that number of people in the places that it was said. Now, there are a number of reasons for that, but we generally had difficulty in saying yes there are 10.000 or 5.000. There were moments when I went looking for these people, and I rarely was able to find the sort of numbers that were being described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Why was it difficult to estimate or determine the number of internally displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, what tended to happen was that if there was military or police action in a particular area, it's quite possible that the inhabitants of that village would -- would decide to leave for reasons of safety, but they wouldn't form themselves into a column and march down the road. They would go to the first place where they felt safe. And if they had relatives in the next village or the next village on, then they would drop in to those relatives who would open their houses to them. And so the further you were from the scene of some fighting, the less people you could find on the road because they would generally have found shelter as close to -- to their point of departure as possible -- in the first place they felt safe. And of course many of them would be related to people in the next village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: So it was just very difficult to verify these numbers, and we tried not to just repeat them blindly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- the KVM then evacuated Kosovo on the 20th of March. When were you told that you were going to evacuate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think it was late in the afternoon of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so you evacuated on the 20th, and where did the KVM go?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We drove out into Macedonia. We paused in Macedonia to make sure we had everybody, because obviously there were nearly 1400 of us and about 500 vehicles. And then we went, according to a pre-arranged plan, mainly down to Lake Ohrid where there was sufficient accommodation to put everybody up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you were -- had evacuated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you actually said there was a pre-arranged location - is that right? - rather than town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, "a pre-arranged town," but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Lake Ohrid had a complex of large hotels around it, and we lobbed into there -- sorry, we settled into there. But we'd worked out where we had to go. We knew how many beds we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, after you had evacuated, did you go up to the border zone?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. About a hundred people stayed up in Skopije at the start in order to remain close to the seat of power in Macedonia in order to do diplomatic business and to be ready to go back in because we were all convinced that we were going to be turning around and going back in within a small number of days. So about a hundred of us stayed in that area, and as -- as events unfolded on the border, we were there straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What did you see at the border? Can you describe what you saw up there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: The border was specifically the main crossing point from Kosovo into -- into northern Macedonia, and it was, therefore, the main point into -- the main point that people would come into Macedonia from Serbia. And there rapidly built up large numbers of what were then refugees who had been ejected or had themselves elected to leave -- to leave Kosovo, and hence to leave Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look at Exhibit P2541, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Zoom in on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, can you explain the Court what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: This is a briefing document made for me by all of the staff which was a summary of what we understood to be going on inside Kosovo at the time based on all of the contacts that we had made with people by mobile phone or by talking to people as they came over the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was this document used for?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I was ordered back to the UK for 24 hours by my minister of foreign affairs so that I could brief him at first hand on what was going on. And so I got my people to produce the best summary they could of what they knew to be going on while discounting the things that they felt were not able to be verified. And so everything on here had been got from more than one source so as to eliminate the wild reporting that was very -- very rife at the time. We were trying to get the most balanced view that we could of what was going on. There was a lot more wild stuff than this going on. This was the stuff we felt was verifiable in terms of the reliability of the source and the credibility of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to show you the next exhibit on our list which is P2542. You might remember this document while we are getting it up. It's -- I believe it's a press statement that you gave or your note for a statement you gave after your meeting with the foreign secretary is now [indiscernible]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In this briefing, if we look at pages -- at the bottom of page 3 or maybe we can just go to the last page, actually. Sorry. There you refer to some numbers of refugees. Am I correct that K stands for kilo, a thousand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We were at this stage measuring refugees in thousands. We had -- obviously when we said 7.000 we had seen 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you also consider these refugee numbers as being a correct reflection of what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you return to Kosovo later on in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I accompanied the NATO force when it re-entered Kosovo on D-Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what date was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I think it was the 13th of June, but it may have been the 12th. I think, actually, it was the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you returned, did you see any attempts at destroying documents, mostly ID documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes. I came across a smoldering, what I thought was a bonfire, outside the main police headquarters on the evening of D+1, and I was in company with Colonel Richard Ciaglinski. And we stood looking at this smoldering bonfire, which was about 3 feet high, and was all ash on the outside. And it took us a few moments to realise that this was actually a pile of documents that was burning down, and I think it was only when one or other of us kicked it that we -- we realised that in the middle of this were a number of identity -- it was entirely comprised of identity documents that were being burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph to make sure that we're not getting something --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, Mr. Ivetic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: A couple of points, Your Honour. First of all, I'm looking through the statement given by this witness and I'm unable to find this testimony being disclosed anywhere, as a preliminary point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the exhibit in question that is now I believe being tendered to the witness, that was only disclosed to us on Friday, not previously, and I would object because there's been no foundation as to where exactly this publication comes from. And I'm a little bit confused as to why it was not disclosed to us prior to the cross-examination of Colonel Ciaglinski because I would have utilised it at that point in time, and I believe now I will want to be calling Mr. Ciaglinski back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just one quick addition to what Mr. Ivetic said. The text of 2538 we respectfully suggest is certainly not admissible. It's another question about the two pictures, which I don't think Your Honour wants to hear argument about now, but I think the text -- and perhaps Mr. Marcussen will voluntarily withdraw it because I don't think it has any business being in this case. I see him nodding in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, we don't intend to rely on the text of the document and that probably shouldn't have been included in the exhibit in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That will be withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So we can withdraw those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, one other thing before we get too far. 2541 no objection was made when the witness was testifying, but I do think that's the DZ bullet points of 1 April 1999. It's sort of a mini As Seen, As Told, and I would respectfully note an objection to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's different from As Seen, As Told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a second until I note what was in there. This is a document which is not one of the attached exhibits, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have P2541 up again because I can't remember the bullet point that's being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can this be enlarged a little so that it can be read? Now, Mr. Sepenuk, what is the point that you're taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, the point is that most of the items described in here, Your Honour, come from other unnamed, unverifiable sources, obviously not under oath, and they're being reported by General DZ. And I think it's totally unreliable and, as I say, akin to the As Seen, As Told situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Particularly looking at, for example "current situation, human interest refugee stories."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this objection comes too late and your arguments will need to be reflected on a question of weight because the witness gave evidence that this was verifiable information that had been condensed down to verifiable information, and on that basis the Chamber has followed its normal practice in the absence of objection it's been admitted. So it's now for you to deal with it as a question of weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far as the other matter is concerned there's a question of disclosure raised, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The document was provided to the Defence if not the day we got the document, then the day after. As soon as we got this document from the general, we provided a copy to the Defence. So we have done this as quickly as we could. The general mentioned during proofing that he might have some pages that could be of assistance. He very kindly copied these pages and sent them to us. So we simply didn't have them formerly disclosed to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, with respect to the pile of documents, I'm unsure about whether or not these documents are actually the same as the one that the witness saw. So there might not even be an issue. And actually what I intended to do was to try to find out whether or not the picture is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean not the same as Ciaglinski saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As the general saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I'm under the impression they're actually not the same, in which case we should clarify that and then there is no issue maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes and no. Is your objection, Mr. Ivetic, only to the text or is it also to the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the objection to the text is I think the same as Mr. Sepenuk stated. The text of the partial document that was given to us has nothing to do with these photographs and talks about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's been withdrawn --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the question of re-calling a witness is a matter for you -- for you to raise. But the second issue, is your objection also to the photographs being used to clarify the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And the initial objection was to the point that there has been no disclosed testimony of this witness relating to seeing any pile of documents, and therefore I'm a little confused as to where this comes up all of a sudden. And then of course, as I indicated, this -- I don't know whether the witness took this photograph -- he's definitely not pictured in it, so I don't know how he can testify as to what it shows absent to one of those two items, because otherwise the proper person to ask about this picture would be Colonel Ciaglinski, since he's the only one I see in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the overall context of the case, we consider this evidence to be rather a matter of detail. It would be no surprise that it would not be particularly referred to in a 65 ter summary. The -- it's unfortunate, as you've constantly heard me commenting, that the Prosecution have not carried out investigations in this case at a stage which would have enabled them to identify this sort of thing earlier and disclose it. But it doesn't seem to us that any prejudice will be caused in relation to the use of this -- these particular photographs, and therefore we'll permit them to be presented to the witness. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: General, I believe you know which photograph we are talking about, a photograph of a gentleman sitting among some ID documents. Without looking at the document, are you able to tell us whether or not this is -- the pile in that photograph is the pile of ID documents that you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I am almost positive it is not. I am almost a hundred per cent positive it is not because of the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So we will withdraw that from -- that's what I was actually intending to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So we will withdraw that as well from this exhibit. So what remains is one photograph of a MUP soldier and the rest of that exhibit is out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can leave that dead-end and proceed to another route, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, actually, on this high note the Prosecution ends its direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. On the question of the police headquarters in Pristina that we thought we were about to have a look at, in your statement at paragraph 23 you refer to two police headquarters in Pristina, the public police headquarters and then the main police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These were two separate buildings, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The building outside which I came across the pile of smoldering documents was the public headquarters, not what I could call the administrative and operational headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a building that was damaged by bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, can you tell me the order in which questions will be asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Ojdanic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that this evidence is made up of two elements: The oral evidence of the witness and the statement and associated exhibits. But there is much in the statement that's not of prime importance in the overall context of the case. By the end of tomorrow, cross-examination and evidence in chief will have amounted to about very similar times. It may be that we should have most of it done, if not all of it done, by then, depending on how things are focused and depending on what we decide about the document that we haven't yet dealt with, the blue book. But I think you should proceed on the assumption at the moment that you don't need to go into that. It will be clearly directed in the opposite direction first thing tomorrow if it is otherwise. So let's see how we can get on with focused cross-examination. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's my understanding that the -- the Prosecutor has two witnesses this week, and in anticipation that the cross-examination of this witness would be fairly long, and I suppose if we speed up with this witness then, we're going to finish early and get some time off. But I think there's important stuff that a lot of people want to deal with with this witness. I intend, on the other hand, to be fairly -- fairly brief with regard to this witness, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good. Let's start.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, my name's John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this case. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you first about some of the testimony you've given today. At page 65 of your evidence today - and you'll remember this because it was just a few moments ago - you were talking about the harassment of Albanians by -- primarily by Serb police, I think, and how -- how they would just harass them over and over and over. And the question I have of you was -- is that it's true, is it not, that the KLA was similarly engaged in the harassment of Serbian civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact -- actually, more than harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at Exhibit P444, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First of all, I take it you will recognise that as an official document from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- it's one that I had made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go to the -- I think it's the fourth page of that document; it's got 3069 is the number at the top. Yes, it's the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Incidents of kidnap and abduction continue." Contains this kind of information: "On 27th February, three Serbian men were abducted in the Prizren region. On 27 February, two Serb brothers were abducted near the village of Velika Hoca south of Orahovac. The KLA first admitted to holding the men but then distanced themselves from the incident. One of the hostages was beaten to death by the KLA. The other abducted person was released alive but having been severely beaten. 3rd March, two Serb civilians shot and killed by the KLA at a check-point in the village of Mijalic located between on Prizren and Vucitrn. On 9th March, Prizren regional centre reported that an Albanian from Tirana was abducted by a group of masked men wearing black uniforms with KLA insignia. The police said the Albanian was a civilian working as a document clerk in the Prizren police station. The KLA indirectly confirmed their involvement and the OSCE started negotiations to secure his release." So not only were they harassing, they were killing and beating Serb civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly make pauses between questions and answers for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 73 of the transcript today, it's I think at line 21, you were being asked about basically your view of the way that the Serb forces were approaching the problem of the KLA. And you used this language that the -- the -- maybe not exactly this language, but that their retaliation was the best recruiting sergeant for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that if you just look at our experience in the world with anti-terrorist operations, most frequently any anti-terrorist operation is a good recruiting sergeant for the terrorists, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. It depends on the way that it's conducted and the way it's described and the overall sense of justice and obedience to the laws that is carried out by the forces of the state. There are two standards here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you go after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. You're both quite quickly in on top of the end of the preceding speaker and we have an interpretation problem now. It was working very well with Mr. Marcussen and Mr. Drewienkiewicz, and it would be helpful if you both observed a pause just to allow the interpretation to catch up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you go after terrorists, no matter how you do it, it tends to encourage other people to join them. Now, if you can find an exception somewhere in the modern world to that proposition, maybe you can tell us what it is. But I'm thinking of the Russians in Chechnya, I'm thinking of the UK and the US in Iraq, which has been a great recruiting poster for al-Qaeda, I'm thinking of the UK in Northern Ireland, which did a pretty good job of recruiting for the IRA for a while. Can you come up with an example in the modern world where restraint has lessened terrorist activity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't think I would characterise the operations in Northern Ireland as being in any way similar to what we're looking at here. I would strongly refute that. I think that -- I don't think we're here to discuss Northern Ireland, but I am here to discuss what I saw on the ground and my reaction to it. And I'm quite clear that there is a different standard for an insurgent operation that is fighting against the organs of a state, for whatever reasons, and the way that the organs of the state respond to it. And if they descend to the same level, then they delegitimatise themselves, and I think that that's what we teach in the military academies and which we attempt, as best we can, to follow, not always successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you didn't answer my question, but you are trying to legitimatise terrorists by calling them insurgents, and the KLA terrorists certainly were not insurgents, and we'll get to that a little more probably tomorrow about that. But tell me an example in the modern world where restraint, the kind of restraint you're suggesting, was effective against terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I would say in Northern Ireland where in every case possible we took evidence and we charged the people and we put them in jail. And that was a better response than shooting them in cold or hot blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Any others, or is that the only one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I would need -- I would need some -- some notice of the question but I think I could probably find several more as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I don't think they are parallels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go to another subject then. At page 74 you told us that it was your estimate that the number of actual KLA fighters was several hundred in Kosovo while you were there. Did I --

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- quote that properly? And when you say "several hundred," I assume that you mean less than a thousand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would that have been the case in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was getting greater then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But would it have been the case in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I would have said there was still less than a thousand --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you kindly again bear in mind that we're interpreting what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're doing a very bad job, General, at pausing. We need to try much better -- to do that much better. If the Chief of the General Staff of the KLA told us that there were 17.000 or 18.000 soldiers in the KLA in Kosovo, that some of those were involved in logistics but there were 17 or 18.000, I take it you would defer to him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You were asked about -- I think it had to do with the situation at Racak, and Judge Bonomy asked you if you could see the -- the VJ on the hills; you mentioned they were on the hills. Judge Bonomy asked you if you could see them, and you said you could; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, that was an area called -- I think it was called Dulje hill. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Dulje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that was a place where the VJ always was. They had a permanent facility there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: They had a position on the -- on the Dulje heights, but I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about ridge lines much closer to the village than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they were always there at the Dulje heights; that's really my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a couple of kilometres further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked this morning about your observation as you made your trip around Kosovo and looked at the damage that had been done to the houses and villages and told us that it was your opinion that that damage had been done by arson rather than combat.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it that -- that you must have seen some instances of houses that had been hit by small-arms fire or machine-gun fire or something like that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But apparently it's your position that the vast majority at least were arson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That was the impression I gained at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I take it you saw few, if any, that had been destroyed by what -- what might have been artillery fire or something like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: At the time, it was -- it appeared to be mainly small-arms fire or direct hits from tank main armament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let me go, then, to another issue. You were talking about the lack of absorption during the OSCE mission of US-KDOM and EU-KDOM, and I think your actual words were because they were all over the place and creating confusion. And you said that the Serb authorities were irritated by that and that you were also irritated by that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P658, which you will recognise as the agreement on the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission -- I've got to find the right spot. It's paragraph 5 right there on the first page. "KDOM will act in place of the OSCE Verification Mission pending its establishment. Once OSCE is operational, KDOM will be absorbed by the verification mission." That was part of the agreement, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us this morning that US-KDOM basically refused to be absorbed and continued to operate throughout that process?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you provide any reports regarding that and by that violation of the agreement? Did you report that to the United Nations or anyone else that the United States and you were violating the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Sadly, I wasn't in charge of the United States at the time and I still am not, but on a -- to be serious, of course we did. It was something which I consistently brought up. It was not just the US-KDOM, it was the EU-KDOM. Both of them continued to get under our feet and complicate issues in a way that was unhelpful to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if I were to look in the OSCE reports to the UN Security Council, I should find a report of violation regarding paragraph 5 of the beginning of this agreement here on page 1?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I was not writing the reports to the United Nations Security Council. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I certainly made no secret of the fact that it was irritating and it was, as I say, not just the US-KDOM, it was the EU-KDOM that was as irritating.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you just for a moment about this helicopter issue. I think one person, maybe even -- maybe even it was the French diplomat that was the number two person in the mission, Gabriel Keller, took the position that -- that you or General Walker or somebody was too focused on the helicopter and it deterred you from your mission. You spent all your time worrying about the helicopter. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I would say that it became something of a cause celebre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An obsession almost.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That isn't my word. We were -- every time we brought it up, we were asked for more details by the Serb authorities, which we then provided. It was important to us because it affected the perception in Vienna of the safety of the verifiers, and they felt very strongly about it up in Vienna. And if they thought their verifiers weren't safe, they weren't going to provide them and we weren't going to get the mission built up as quickly as we wanted it to be built up, as everybody wanted it to be built up. So, yes, it was important. It had a symbolic issue. It was the first area in which we had a very straight refusal from the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt and let's just pause for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What explanation were you given for this refusal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The explanation that was given -- it wasn't really an explanation. It was a, No, you can't. The -- in the context, it -- the statement was made that -- and I think it was by Mr. Sainovic, that of course once you're in the helicopter you can use it for all sorts of other activities. You can use it to spy on the situation on the ground, which we were not really concerned about because NATO had carte blanche to patrol above Kosovo and take as many photographs as they wished, and there was nothing more we would be able to do from a helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it was a fear of abuse that was the reason given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only reason that was given, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the case, isn't it, that you were offered a helicopter and that you could paint it any way you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We were offered a helicopter of considerably less capability --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just answer my question. You were offered a helicopter that you could paint any way you wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Not that we could paint, no. It would have been -- it would have been remained in the colour at which it was offered to us and would not have been able to be distinguished from any other Yugoslav aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if it was a white helicopter with a big red cross on it, you would still reject it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was never offered like that, but the answer would probably have been yes, because one of the reasons we'd painted our vehicles orange was to make sure that they were different from the white vehicles and the blue vehicles and the green vehicles that the Serb forces were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ask if it could be painted orange?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your rejection of that helicopter apparently was based, by your own testimony, on your understanding of the KLA as a -- as an organisation that would be very likely to try to shoot down a medevac helicopter. True?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: That would be very likely that would want to shoot down a Yugoslav helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A medevac helicopter marked with red cross markings, white?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't -- I did not put great faith in their ability to not shoot at something if they thought that it was a Yugoslav helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we end up with here is the idea that the Albanians won't trust a Yugoslav helicopter, and that the Serbs won't trust an OSCE helicopter. That's what we've got, isn't it, and we're spending an awful lot of time on this. Let's move on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You say in your supplementary statement, and that's at paragraph 5, (v): "The Serb military strategy did not work because the Serbs did not separate or isolate KLA from the civilian population even though most Kosovo Albanians did not support the KLA." Doesn't this go a long way to convincing you that the KLA was truly a terrorist organisation not even supported by most of the Albanian people?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's -- that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Shouldn't the international community have joined with the Serbs and the Albanian people of Kosovo that did not support the KLA to rid Kosovo of this terrorist scourge rather than supporting and protecting them, as they did? Wouldn't that have been the proper way to go about dealing with the problem of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: We neither supported nor protected the KLA. And we went there to attempt to make the situation better, which would -- which meant buying time so that the Serb authorities who were the sovereign state there could put their house in order and stop alienating their population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, after having told us in the first part of that paragraph that the Serbs did not separate or isolate the KLA from the civilian population, you then tell us they were not prepared to take the fight to the KLA up in the hills where they were. Now, that sounds inconsistent to me. They were either separated from the civilian population or they weren't.

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: Isn't that inconsistent? You're saying at one point they didn't separate them from the civilian population and then immediately you're saying they wouldn't take the fight in the hills to where the KLA was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: It was my impression that the Serbs were not prepared in the December, January, February time to attempt to go to where the KLA were and only the KLA were and deal with them there. They were much more prepared to go to where the interface was between the KLA semi-controlled areas and the Serb semi-controlled areas. If you want to wipe out terrorists or insurgents, you go after where they are, not where they might be. And it is difficult, because they all look the same. And a Kosovar Albanian in civilian clothes might be a KLA member who's taken his uniform off. I understand that perfectly. That's the problem that security forces have, and it's a problem all security forces have and they have to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And whether they're guerillas or terrorists or insurgents or whatever that doesn't make much difference in that context, does it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Well, they don't conveniently wear pink hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. I want you to look at another exhibit, and before I do that, it's just -- you know, I look at the reports of the OSCE, especially those that were filed with the Security Council, and it appears that the situation in Kosovo was gradually improving with the efforts that were being made by the OSCE mission, that the incidents of violations were diminishing and that things were getting better. And I get that from a lot of places, but for instance if we look at P636, and I don't know if you're familiar with this document. I guess you are because it was an annex to your statement. There's a table attached to this document, a several-page table. And without having it in your hand, it's probably going to be difficult for you to follow, but I just did a quick counting or a not-so-quick counting. The table covers the last 11 days of January and the first 13 days of February. Now, if you look at that table, what you'll find out is in the last 11 days of January there were 13 violations by KLA and 25 by FRY; two of the FRY violations were access violations. The total number of incidents was 38. If you then go to February, where you've got two more days, there were ten KLA violations and only nine FRY violations, and all of those were access violations, the total being only 19 violations or half as many in more days in February. So this report to the UN would -- leads one to believe that your mission was meeting with success and that the incidents were diminishing and that everything was working well, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
utterances.text: Let me try to give you a long answer, if I may, because I think yes/no answers don't work here. Firstly, what -- who decided compliance. The head of the mission and then the OSCE in Vienna decided what was and what wasn't compliance, and it was very important that we did not accuse people of non-compliance before it had been agreed at the mission headquarters that it was or wasn't so that there was a common standard. And therefore, what was compliance, what was judged to be compliance, was taken very, very seriously, and it didn't involve minor things. The second thing is that not every incident is of equal weight. The events at Rogovo that I saw were at quite a different level of violence to whether or not somebody could go into a barracks or not. The third thing is that during this period we were leading up -- we were first of all dealing in the -- the aftermath of Racak when there was a notable sensitivity on everyone's part. Secondly, we were dealing with the start of the Rambouillet talks, and everyone involved attempted to restrain themselves. And, as you would expect, the official forces of the state did what they were told. That I would have expected. And so during that period, the first half of February, the level of instance did go down and we reported it as such. And when it went up again, we reported it as such. So, yes, it did go down, but those were the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you that weight is important, and when you look at those first 13 days in February, every violation by FRY was an access denial. Nine violations by KLA were either shooting at FRY forces, three of those; there were ambushes and killings, six of those; and only one access. So weight is important, and the weight there indicates the major violators were KLA, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN DREWIENKIEWICZ
